TY-e3ide has been very gay of late. H,r Majesty's appearances have been exceptionally frequent,and every- day Royal personages ridi Je or driving in the vacinity of Balmoral, have been en evidence. This year. as last the Queen drives gray horses, wuwh give a livel-r tone to her equlpag.4. Rubber tires too have evidently come to stay in thoi Royal stable, these having now been at- tached to all the Queen's carcia.o3. Invercauld, which the Sovereign frequently honours with a visit,when the Court is at Balmoral, is one of the most b. autifully situated places in the Highlands. The present owner is Mr. Farquharsin, heir presumptive to the Baronetly of R'JS3 of Balnagowen. As most people ate aware,Her Majesty honours Mr. and Mrs. Farquhar- son with her favour and friendship, and this she ex- tends to their present tenants Mr. and Mrs. Neumann. The latter is a very pre;ty woman, slight, dark-haired, and possessed of beautiful eyes, and s fine complexion. She speaks English with perfect correctness, and has be- come in recent yeas one of th most admired hostesses in London.

The Queen of Hanover, mother of the Duko of Cum- berland, who not long since celebrated her eigkt:eth year, is, it is said, showing signs of failing health. Of a most genial temperament, the Queen is greatly beloved by all her children, grandchildren, ab 4 relations, beside the large number of old friends, servants,and adherents, who are at out her. She is a very clever woman, and keeps herself abrest of European politics and literature, Her domeric arrangem .nta ar:A simple in the extreme. —Dinner at two, and supp.r at seven o'clock. There is a general lea tnat Royal folk, iike Lucullus of old, feast every day, but such is not the case. Though rich dinners are provided !ro • visitors and offioials, many Crowned Heads, and memb qs of Royalty partake of the simplest food only. Our Qujea always 14 ppPars at the elaborate nine o'clock dinner for the Court, but it is seldom that she touches any but the plainest (lister, sad of them she partakas most sparingly. Tho Emperor of , Austria too, is satisied wt•h the simplest food, provided It be well cooked. _ . _

WRY THE PIG WAS NOT Kir...Lnn.—A certain schoolmaster in a village school had been in the habit of purchasing pork from parents of his pupils on the occasion of the killing of the pig. One day a small boy marched no to the master's desk, and inquired "if he would like a bit of pork as they were going to kill their pig." The schoolmaster replied in the affirmative. Several days having elapsed, and hearing nothing of the pork the master called the boy up to him, and inquired the reason he had not brought it. What was the surprise of the master when the boy replied: "Oh, please, sir, the pig got better."

I feel now, in the light of the manly and sincere declara- tion you have just made to me, that I was perhaps wrong in encouraging all those attentions wnich I attributed more to your naturally chivalrous nature than I did to the strong current of genuine love. I listened, as any foolish girl does, to the sentiments you expressed, thinking that they were due to the freedom of the sea- shore, and falsely giving them a much lighter estimate than I know now you meant them for. Forgive me, pray, if I have misunder- stood the depth and sincerity of your character. I feel, alas! that beside you I am indeed un- worthy ; but, believe, , me. as I have said, that I did not dream of this.' div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR Nzia,n,

September is quite the transition month of fashions, and although the unusual spell of hot weather has enabled folks to wear their summer hats and dresses longer than usual, yet moderately warm costumes and coats must soon be necessary for evenings and chilly days. Woollen materials are very desirable because falling dew and sale breezes fail to make them limp, and there is noth- ing more . disagreeable than the clamminess characteristic of cotton fabrics under such cir- cumstances.

A pretty little bonnet, is made of tnrcluoise vel- vet, with wings of ehemille sewn with jet sequins or either side, and a high , white jetted osprey in front, secured with a handsome tuira•like ornament of paste and silver. For autumn toques crumpled straw is used, trimmed with wired velvet and a knot of flowers in front. It is wonderful how the straw is pinched into shape. Two colours, such as a lnont straw with Po mixture of red, or green and grey are much in vogue and have a very smart effect. Tho ribbon velvet used with a wired back to keep it twisted in shape is quite narrow, and brilliant touches of colour arc managed with its help. The autumn hats are allowed a little contrast between the straw and the trimming.

Just now Dame Fashion, like the rest of the world, is taking a holiday, and in the matter of dress accords her new inspirations grudgingly, if at all. On one point alone ca; rho be prevailed upon to give utterance with anything like ch.:finite- ness, and that is on the subject of furs and fur gar- ments, in which the modes of the ; uture are already beginning to declare themselves. An admirable sealskin coat, in what is likely to be one of the favourite shapes for next winter, which is of moderate length, double-breasted and finished with revers and storm collar of Russian sable; the buttons are of a novel pattern, made in smoked mother-of-pearl, covered with gold filagree, and the lining is of rich brocade. . .

A most useful wrap at the present time is a smart coat that can be worn with any drug. The most fashionable cut is the long swallow tail, the backs of which reach about three•quarters of the way down the skirt. There is a long rounded basque that fits closely over the hips, while the fronts are rounded off or cut away. The plainer the outlines of these coats the better, though they are sometimes cut in turrets. The best colours are silver grey or almond-tinted cloth, either of which look extremely well with black skirt, shoes, and hat. Very useful early autumn costumes are grey figured alpaca coats and skirts with grey or white vests.

A fashionable coat and skirt has the latter plain, but beautifully cut, and the coat of the short Ches- terfield type, has the strapped seams finished with five rows of stitching, and the high roll collar, that may be worn either up or down, and the smart, sharp-pointed revere are faced with mink. This costume looks well carried out in beaver cloth. An extremely stylish bodice of grass la-vn which can be worn with almost any skirt. The lawn is stamped out in an all-over design specially adapted for bodice or jacket, sleeves and collar, all the openings edged with cord, and made up over white satin. About the height of the bust there is a series of openings through which black satin ribbon is inserted, and the rosette, V below the throat, and sash are black satin. The vest is white silk. Such a bodice as this is most welcome for a watering place promenade on a hot sunshiny morning. Many of the new kid gloves show glaring trans- gressions of conventional ideas, and illustrate the disregard which fashion has for economy. The long-popular, useful, and always appropriate fawn, brown, and tan-coloured gloves for general wear are not to be altogether abandoned by fashionable women, but their place is largely taken by a host of odd, conspicuous shades—green, purple, orange, dahlia, and begonia colours, with reproductions in paler tints for evening wear. Most ot the buttons on gloves are large and showy, and the stitching contrasting and striking. Your loving Jimmy.

THE BANISTERS.—The banister is a part of the house woodwork that requires frequent attention. This rail should first be wiped off with a wet cloth. Mix two parts of linseed oil with one part of tur- pentine; apply this to the railing, then polish it with a fresh flannel. _ _

His Majesty rises at five, be-akfasts on a cup of strong coffee, and a plate of cold meat.' 'Hs then ahstaics from fcoi till twelve, when lunch is served, consisting of two courses, soup and roast meat. At three he dines off five courses—sonp, fish, roast, podding, dessert. he is very . fond of puddings, and in puddings Austrian cooks excel. The Sovereign does not break his fast until the following morning at five. Wen a State function takes Once, however, the sole rdour and laviihness ot the Imperial table knows no bounds, and do t fifteen co iters hide tit-bits floaa ev ry nattonaliy, ace ortling to the tats of His Malesty'a guests. Although womsri ..f late yells hays made wonderful strides in the art of dining, aad no loiiger see fit to feel ashamed of a healthy appetite. many are still apt to go astray, in the matter or prop ait meals. when their men folks happen to be absent. Whim thn master of the house dices out alone, the mistress seldom orders for her selt a proper dinner, but has " something on a tray." generally an egg, and tea and bread and butter. There is a story of a little boy who Once asked his mother what God had for dinner. " G.iel never diners, you should not ask such irreverent questions," ws,X the reply. The little one was quiet for a while, end then said thought- fully, remerabning the custom in his own home, " Oh, I suppose he has an egg with- his tea:" ' Many a serious breekdown in health is du a to neglect of proper feeding. Busy working women, living *llene are of cowed, the clef offenders in this respilee. They neglect often to lay 'a sold f-undatinn for the day at breakfast, and at eleven o'clock they resort to tea and a biscuit, to stave off that " tired feslng "which we read of in adveitisements. Instead of a wholesome and simple lunch, they consume a bun and a glass of milk, or perchance more tea, and so on throughout the day. Thus they give their digestive organs COEStant work,with the minimum of profit to their system. A busy Woman needs three good meals a day, one on no account should she indulge in the constant nibbling system which like dram drinking, ruins the health. In choosing a dinner table the housewife should bear in mind two items—that it should,if possible, be round, and—rot toe !arm A round table, at which each diner can see all his other fellows. lea great promoter of pleas- ant talk. In the matter of ciscoration, the fashion of the moment is for heliotrope, red, or yellow, and as re garde flowers, chrysanthemums are in high favour. These blossoms seem to grow more beautiful with every year that passes, and their enormous variety of tint also seems to be increasing. F There are the yellow flowers, the shade of which is ito 11 the brightest and most cheerful tone, that which always reminds one of the Chinese name f or yellow "the dau ?to- ter of light." Then there are, the deep crimson chryiarr then:Mins—the edges of the psta's just touched with fawn—which light us up :most exquisitely. Thew re. quire- el course, the relief of maidenhair rr some light leaf, snch as asparagus tops, to which we owe euch debt of gratitude for their graceful abundance. Pure white chrysanthemums seem to grow to a larger size than colored, and their thousand petals have • acli a different form. It is worth examiu rig one of these tn note the extraordinary variety. Net even taii o are e iged alike, and the effect of the levels' flowers is eno:rn eddy enhanced by this infinite difference. Slippers as flower-vases have disappeared from th dinner table, an item to congratulate ourselves upen. The association of shoes and food is not an agreeable idea, end then there is the old superstition n ahut plac- ing boots and shoes upon a table. It is a rnis'ak to put before guests what may make them uncomfortable in relation to any soner+Wion thee may have ehere.hed, and is there one of us whe has not s -me weak point in this connectien - .

„ Eldsrly women WEI patren"sing grey very much this actumn,and the value of the t nt to the grey-haire 1 is beyond estimatices. One modish matron I rye', when paying a call a few afterngons back, was a picture. She wore a black transparent canvas grenadine skirt over erey silk, a black silk coat, and a dainty liia grey bonnet, with fluffy grey tulle strings, that just suited her-silvers`ouched wavy hair. And this reminds me, by the way, that to keep Pace with modern notions, the elderly matronlionest visit. the hairdresser just as regularly as he daughter or grand- daughtsr, for the mysteries of hairdressinr. & woman of my acquaintance. °toning blilae:y to ‘ixty snmmers has her silver locks skilfully waved every week. Not that she has an elabrrate and foolishly fashionable coiffure. Her hair is p sited c'early over the for haad, brushed down each aide, and braided at the back modestly enough to please the most conservative no- tions. Only the hair ripples down most naturally over the face and that makes all the difference. Apropos of calls, on might have supposed that the glaring silliness to which the institution hae aulk,would long since have driven practical people to find a way • ut. But if no calls were paid, how, it is sometimes asked, could we see anything of our frierde ? Sanc'a &mom. tas ! Who ever pays call, a bona fide cal% with the idea of seeing their friends ? The true 'caller ” stria in her carriage, with a " Court Geife," and a stet of n sse paper toll of tames, and tru ti to get throueh them all in an afternoona mercifully favoured with a high per- centage of" outs." A friend found at home is a disas- ter. A lost ten minutes is a serioos matter, specially if the caller has to b3ar in mind that her carriAge is "by the hour." But in such a case, there is no help font. The caller deceeds, greets her hostess. "so delighted to land her at home," and spends the remaining time in firing off a few conversatioral blank cartridges among other callers who may or may not be acquaintances of her own, or in the intellectual exercise, of mentally putting a price to their hats. Then when she laAs touched her hostess's fingers with a gra' ()fall ackno xledcement of the great pleasure cf her call, and has left the ne-essary cards in the hall, she escapes to the free air of heaven and her hired victoria. A whole class or society thus teils on for ever at the social treadmill, calling, calling, calling,and with beautiful resignation day after day, gets through "the trivial round, the common task." Furs have again put in appearance and the newest models are scarcely as fascinating as one could desire. Some of the capes are ugliness itself. Flung on a skele- ton they would look bulky while on a woman of moder- ate erre:aortic-ins, the effect is m-re easily imagined than described. Entire gowns of fur are, it is said, to obtain great success later on. It is t he hoped, if this pronh- , ecy prove cortect,that the au'hsrities will arrange with the clerk of the weather to provide us with an ade- quately severe winter. (CoPrigAL)
A WARD OF THE KING.
By KATHARINE S. MACQUOID, Author of "Maisie Derrick," "The Story cor Lois, "Patty," "Louisa, "At the Red Glove," "Miss Eyon of Eyoncourt," Scc.
CHAPTER XXV. THE CROSSING Or THE RHONE.

The Constable and his faithful friend had acted wisely in leaving the house on foot, for the sound of horses would have reached Laval's ears as he approached the inn. Muffled in their dark riding- cloaks, the two fugitives moved on swiftly in the d irkness till they reached the first little hamlet beyond the hill. They paused at the door of a larger cottage than the rest. Their arrival was evidently expected. The woman who opened the door to them no sooner saw the Duke's tall figure than she turned to the lad behind her. "Bring out the horses, Desire," she said, "but not to the front; the messieurs will mount in the yard. Start one off some minutes before the other; that one "—she pointed to Bourbon—" must take the road on the right, the other the lane that leads left; they will meet at the fork by the water- trough outside the village." ' She moved aside that the new-comers might enter the,: house, she did not speak to them, but as the Duke passed her on his way to the back door, she knelt down and pressed the hem of his cloak to her lips. • In the yard were two horses, bridled and saddled. Desire held up,a lantern he had taken from the stables, and Bourbon saw that they Were powerful animals, and also that a piece of armour was round their chests. The lad who held them did not look at ,the Duke, but when Monsieur de Pomperant had held his companion's stirrup, and then had vaulted into his own saddle, Desire pressed close to him and whispered: "Monsieur will find provisions for two days in the saddle-bags. Five la justice ! " De Poniperant smiled kindly. "I thank you, friend. When next we meet, matters may have changed. I will not forget you, Desire."

A hoarse whisper came in answer. "My, lerd must beware. The Rhone is closely guarded at far down as Valence; there is no safe passage this side of Vienne." "We loiter!" the Duke cried. "Come on!" and he rode away. 11 De Pomperant also set spurs to his horse, and galloped on alone till he reached the water-trough; then the two fugitives rode on together for, some hours. Just as a faint glimmer shewbd itself in the east, they were challenged by a sentinel on the banks of the Rhone. They were some way from the river, and it was still too 'dark for recognition, so, hazarding a cry of " Vice le Roi " the fugitives rode on, and the sentinel took no further heed of them.

"We are close to the river," said Bourbon. "Why should we not risk a passage? Vienne is a long way off, and it is close to Lyons and the camp." "Pardon me, my lord, but are we not safer near the enemy? T have been told that the Rhone is watched as ,far down as Valence; no one would look for us at Vienne. Once across the bridge of Vienne, a good road leads us into Dauphiny, whereas, so far as I remember hereabouts, on the eastern bank are marshes, without any road across them. The bridge at St. Vanier is known to be guarded; that challenge makes me think it is close by. Shall we not keep further away? We might hide in some wood till evening, rest our horses, and recruit ourselves. How say you, my lord ? " "Have it as you will," Bourbon answered. "If there were more light I would risk the ford; there used to be one at St. Rambert, which cannot be aluch further." • .
"I learnt at St. Bonnet that the stream is greatly swollen," said De Pomperant. "The Rhone has ever shewn herself a turbulent stream to those who brave her."

"Foi de Prince," the Duke exclaimed, "pursuit is more dangerous than the stream! I wish that instead of flying, and leaving that dear child to the mercies of Laval, I had stood my ground and fought it out, with him." "No no, my lord; Mother Tarbes whispered me that Lzlval's swashbuckler, Gaspard, was at hand, and could readily summon a score or two of cut- throats from the pot-house below the hill." "Sol" _ .

The Duke rode on in moody silence towards the wood which De Pomperant pointed :out. They stayed under its shelter till evening fell; then they again rode on along a rough and difficult road, at some little distance from the river, • -

Day was breaking when they approached Vienne. They now rode very carefully, believing that the bridge would be guarded. They were still at some distance from the bridge when Be Pomperant saw on the western bank of the stream a small cabaret, and near it a ferry-boat, seemingly made fast to a post on the river-bank. "Look, ray lord," he said, there is a ferry- boat." As they approached it, some soldiers came;laugh- ing out of the cabaret, and began to descend the river-bank. The two fugitives reined in their horses and waited, fearing they might be observed by the soldiers. The men, however, seemed to be only concerned with the ferry-boat and its fastenings; they soon went up the bank and back to the cabaret. "Now may Heaven be praised," said Do Pompe- rant, "the fellows have gone back to their wine; let us secure the ferry-boat without the loss of a moment."

They quickly dismounted, and left their tired horses to shift for themselves; De Pomperant un- fastened the chain which secured the boat, and sprang into it, but as Bourbon followed him there came a cry from the cabaret. While De Pomperant pushed off by means of the long pole which lay at the bottom of the boat, the Duke looked back; he saw three soldiers running down the bank. A fourth, who looked like the leader of the rest, came hurrying after them, and pointed out to his men a skiff, which had escaped the fugitives' notice, moored below the bank.
"They are coming back!" Bourbon cried. "Bon Dieu! The saints, then, must come to our aid, for we are outnumbered."

‘q•lot so," the Duke answered ; "a noble is worth three meaner men. Strive for your life to cross the stream, while I guard our boat from capture." The leader's loud, clear voice rang out over the water, as the skiff rapidly gained on the heavy ferry-boat. Pardieu, it is Bourbon; two thousand golden crowns to the man who takes him alive!" "Poi de Prince, that shall never be!" The Duke stood up in the ferry-boat, and as the skiff came close he struck with his heavy sword so vehement a blow at the nearest soldier that the man's severed head fell into the water. De Pomperant saw that further flight was use- less; he dropped his pole only just in time to parry a furious thrust aimed at the Duke by the leader of the pursuers. De Pomperant was at the same time wounded in the arm by one of the soldiers; another struck at Bourbon with his halberd, but the Duke parried the thrust, and ran the fellow through the heart. De Pomperant had closid with the leader of the party, and they stood locked together in deadly struggle. Bourbon sprang into the skiff, but the remaining soldier had no mind to share the fate of his comrade; he jumped overboard, and swam ashore. The leader, a man of great strength, had forced De Pomperant back into the ferry-boat; he then turned on Bourbon. after but a few passes the Duke overcame his guard, and pierced him through the throat. The man fell with a heavy groan on to the side of the skiff, and then into the water.

The ferry-boat had drifted some way down stream, in spite of his wound, Be romperant lost no time in reaching the opposite bank. The Duke had escaped injury, and the fugitives made their way iWand as fast as the roughness of the road per- mitted. The Duke had roughly bound up Do Pomperant's arm ; they feared pursuit from soldiers who might have remained in the cabaret, and they made all haste to gain the shelter of a distant wood. At last they reached it and plunged in among the dense leafage. They well knew they were still in danger, and they would so remain until they reached the first outpost of the Imperial army.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVI. AT LAST.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVI. AT LAST.

Rolland had ridden rapidly away from the hostel of La Verite, then more slowly down the hill which he had so lately mounted. It was growing dark, and he had to ride carefully down the rough road. It seemed to him likely that Laval and his men were near at hand, and he was anxious to return to tilt inn as quickly as he could with a suncient

force in protect Jeanne tram the Cuunt's devices. Now that be had seen her, he guessed at his rival's designs. Doubtless Laval would try to get the Ring's consent to marry her, so that when the time of her mourning expired he would possess himself of both' the beautiful heiress and the lands of Longuedec. But Rolland indulged in a happy smile, for, with all Laval's knavery, it seemed to him that Jeanne's courage and spirit would enable her to defy him; she would not submit to be wedded against her will. All at once he heard a movement on the further side of the road and he made out a shapeless figure on horseback, trying, as it seemed, to ride full speed uphill. t "Who goes there ? " he called out, and urged his horse across the road, so as to bar the passage of the shapeless rider, "Ah I may the blessed saints be praised Eh, Mon Dieu I to • think of meeting Monsieur le Vicomte here, hen I made sure he was _on the hill-top, With my clear lady! I pray inylord to i tell me if she is n safe keeping ? " The familiar voice rejoiced D'Orbec. "Your dear lady will be glad enough to see you, Gillonne ; you have left Lao with his fellows down below, have you so, N and, like a brave- hearted woman, have ridden alone in the gloom to seek your lady. Ride up quickly, iny friend;' you cannot miss your way. The inn stands straight before you on the hill-top. I have but now left your mistress in the hostess's parlour." As the woman rode off, he called after her: "Tell your lady I will retains to her on the instant."

This return was not, however, to be as speedy as he had hoped for. When Gillonne quitted Lao, the men gathered round him, listening to the further tidings .he had gleaned in regard to the Constable's flight from Chantelles. Their loud voices in eager talk reached Rolland, but when he saw no forward movement on the part of the horsemen he felt exasperated, for he had bidden them follow him to the inn on the arrival of Lao.

"Silence!" he cried sternly. "You stemd gossiping like a pack of washerwomen, while mischief may be brewing on the hill-top. You, Mathieu and Lao, mount and follow me: the rest can ride up the hill at a slower pace." With that Rolland turned and galloped up the hill. The September moon, which had been com- pletely veiled by gathering clouds, now rose above them, and as he approached the inn a flood of silver light glorified the gloomy aspect of the place. The light enabled D'Orbec to see a side opening which led, as he guessed, to the stable- yard ; he told himself he - would leave his horse there till his followers joined him. While he tethered his horse to the hook in the wall beside the mounting-block, aillonne's exclama- tion had drawn .Laval's eyes to the window which looked on the courtyard. • The Count felt for an instant checkmated, but a 'second glance shewed him that D'Orbec was aldne. He hastened from the little room, closing the door behind him. "Gaspard!" he cried; then seeing that the man had gone back to his liquor, he drew his dagger and struck the hilt sharply-On the side of the drinker's head. Gaspard started up with an oath; then seeing who had struck him, he said : - -

, "'Tis not fair, my lord, to hit a man Unawares; you have well-nigh cracked my skull." Laval sheathed his dagger. "Peace, thou wine swiller ; there will be work to thy taste in a twinkling. Hist! D'Orbec is here alone; thou or I must settle accounts with him; here he comes." The last words were fiercely whispered, for he heard D'Orbec hurrying in by the side entrance, and in another moment he entered the eating-room by the door at its lower end. The Vicomte's blue Ayes blazed with anger at the sight of Laval. He came forward. , "By what right, monsieur, have you deceived and misled the Counte3s Jeanne, so that she has believed herself on the way to Lyons, while you were bringing her into the Auvergne ? " Laval looked at him, and then laughed con- temptuously. He was on fire to pursue the fugitive Constable, yet he shrank from leaving D'Orbec and Jeanne together. He knew it was no longer possible to carry her amy with him. The only way was to provoke a quarrel; he and Gaspard would soon settle matters with l'Orbec.

Rolland reddened with anger. "You do not answer, my lord? I ask again how you dare to practise this deceit on a lady, a ward of the King?" Laval looked Rolland all over with a; sneer then he said in a mocking tc ne : "You wish for the truth, Monsieur? You shall have it. I guide Countess Jeanne's movements by the right which she has herself given me—the right of her affianced husband."

„ Rolland went nearer him, his eyes ablaze. "Liar! You dare not affirm before the Countess that you are her affianced husband?” Laval backed towards Gaspard. The man drew his dagger. "Softly, Monsieur d'Orbec," Laval said; "your words run away with you. For the sake of her good name, I am willing to tie the knot as soon as may be, considering that the lady has journeyed with me as my wife ever since we left Laval." "Treacherous villain!" Rolland drew his sword and dagger. "Draw, I say, and defend yourself!" Laval also drew his sword and dagger, and rushed, impetuously on Rolland, who stood ready to receive his attack. At the first clash of steel, two spectators appeared in the doorway by which Rolland had entered. In his impatience to return to the inn, d'Orbec had rapidly ridden up the hill, while Mathieu and Lao had followed at a slower pace. These two had just arrived in time, for Gaspard had slunk behind the Vicomte, and was about to stab him, when Mathieu caught the fellow's arm, and sent him reeling across the floor. "Nom de diabie ! " cried Lao. "We will have fair play. Fight like a man, old acquaintance." But Gaspard backed away from the swordsmen. Laval's snake-like eyes almost closed with hatred of his opponent; his height and length of arm gave him some advantage. After a few passes, Rolland received a slight wound in the shoulder, and was driven back by the force and rapidity of Laval's attack. His wound helped. Rolland.; he grew cooler; he saw that in this lay, his advaitage he must he wary, and act only( on the defe rsive, while his adversary played out the fiery ardout with which he had begun the fight. Suddenly Laval retreated, stood still a moment, and then hinged forward, in the hope of tOting hie adversary unawares. But Rolland was ready for him. Instead of parrying the stroke, he swerved aside, avoided it, and before his opponent could recover hinisel f he struck his dagger into Laval's shoulder. The Count staggered, and fell to the ground. Rolland was aghast; it seemed to him that his dagger had glanced aside from armour worn under Laval's butt coat. The Vicomte had not mealt to kill his adversary; in his indignation at La ,ar treachery, he had determined to wound him, a ) as to arrest his evil designs in re.ard to Jeanne, as well as to punish the slander he had uttered abut her.

Laval lay motionless, his eyes were closed; and D'Orbec, bent over him intently listening to catch a breath. Then he turned his head towards Gaspard, who stood seemingly stupefied by the result of the duel. "Come here, fellow, and quickly," D'Orbec cried. "Loosen your master's doublet; and you, Lao, stand back to give him air." At the moment when D'Orbec turned his head, Laval rose to one knee, and struck fiercely with his dagger at the back of his adversary. Lao stood so near; that his strong arm caught the Vicomte as he staggered under the force of the blow. Lao placed him gently on the floor, and then tried to staunch the blood that was now flowing from the wound. Mathieu drew his sword, and rushed at Lav%l, who had risen to his feet. "A moi. Gaspard, a inn!: .f" the Count cried; but Mathieu was too quick for him. "Take your wages, foul assassin!" the man shouted, and drove his sword with such force through Laval's body that it came out at the back. The Count reeled and fell backwards on the floor. Gaspard ran up and knelt beside him. He satisfied himself that life was extinct, he then rose up. his face distorted with fury. "Breton pig! thou hast killed him, " he cried to Mathieu, 'tis well for thee that I and my mates have work in hand that will not wait! Thou shalt hang as high as Hainan, and thy master too, if there is life in him to hang." He hurried out of the inn, as the women came rushing in from the further room. Released from her confinement, Jeanne had flung herself into her faithful woman's arms, and then broke down in a hearty fit of crying. Gillonne had petted and soothed the girl as though were her mother, and Jeanne was recovering herself when angry voices and then the clash of swords in the eating-room alarmed the three women. Tiles,' =cunds were heard, too, upstairs:

Anne ~nd Hai:um-17w came dying down wnn !ihriek: of terror. "Be silent. fools! " Gillonne said sternly; "there ,is enough d;sturhance without the help of your acackling. P e tee, I sayl You, Mathurine. [fetch a cup of water from the well; and you, Anne, open the lattice—the dear lady lacks air." it She had kept her arm round Jeanne while she /spoke, for the girl's white, distraught face made , Gillonne fear she would faint. '1 1
Suddenly. Jeanne rose, and made for the door; she heard the clash of steel, and she knew that• Rolland and Laval were fighting. She determined to part them, at whatever risk to herself.

But Gillonne stayed her with imploring words , and gestures, while the more practical hostess placed herself in the narrow doorway, thus making I it impossible for Jeanne to pass her. 11 "By your leave, no, my lady," she said, with a dignity that enforced obedience. "lidit under my roof shall women thrust themselves into the quarrels of men. Besides, it does no.good ; madame's presence would but prove a hindrance, and would, maybe, endanger Monsieur d'Orbec's life."

. Jeanne looked at her, and then stood passive, . while the incesslnt clash of steel seemed, from its rapidity, likely to be soon ended. . A cry from Lao ; then Mathieu's loud execration. Jeanne clasped her hands in agony. A moment later came the dull sound of a fall, followed b Gaspard's curses. The girl broke away from Gillonne's hold, and forced herself past the hostess; she reached the eating-room, and saw but one thing-711,ol1and's ghastly face and closed eyes as he lay stretched on the ground, where Lao had placed him. "0 my love! my murdered love!" she cried, as she fell on her knees and kissed his lips. ,

div.head: CHAPTER XXVII. irßANcozsz DE FOIX.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVII. irßANcozsz DE FOIX.

A man rather above middle height stood in one of the deeply-recessed windows of the Royal palace at Lyons. His legs were singularly long and thin, and to conceal this lack of proportion he wore very large haut-de-chau,sses of deep murrey-coloured velvet, slashed so as to shew white satin puffs bordered with gold embroidery; his doublet was of the same colour as the trusses, but so richly bejewelled and covered with gold embroidery that not much of the velvet was visible; the sleeves were puffed and pinked with white satin, also gold- embroidered ; a narrow lace edging finished the collar of his doublet Above this rose an expressive face, just now Somewhat flushed. His dark eyes wee long and bright; it was, perhaps, their shape that gave them the astute look of intelligence so much more frequent in a Frenchman 'than in an Englishman. He wore his brown hair very short, his beard too was short and pointed. His Moot remarkable' feature, however, was a long thin nose, so aquiline in form .that its point seemed to over- hang his curved upper lip. This, and the lips themselves, in spite of the intelligence of the fore- head and eyes, gave a sensual cast to the face.

A few minute,s passed, while he seemed to reflect on his companion's words; then he turned to the lady who sat near him on a cushioned couch. 1152 soft grey eyes were earnestly fixed on his face as he looked at her.

"Fri de gentilhomme, ma bel'e, have it as you :will anent this wandering fair onel—l know not how to call her; she is neither wife nor widow; and a wedded damsel is hardly to be termed a maid. Marry her as you will. She is my Ward, and I can dispense with the period of mourning which widow- hood exacts, though methinks a husband but once' seen is hardly to be wept over. • Stay, sweetheart ;' I will grant yet another boon to your proteges ; to the Vicomte d'Orbec I give six months',leave of absence from the , army, so that he ,tnity have time wherein to love and cherish his bride, and see to the revenues of her eetales.. But mark you, sea Tide, he must keep troth when the time has expired he will have to join me in Italy, with a following of at least thirty lances and a good company of foot soldiers. That is, if. I have not .already returned triumphant." Madame de Chateaubriand rose, and bending ono knee to the ground, she kit sed the King's jewelled fingers. "A thousand thanks, my liege, for such goodness to these lovers. You will surely triumph, my King, my hero—you must." Francis raised her very tenderly, and held het an instant, while he gazed lovingly at her fair, sweet face.

"Foi de gentilhomme, ma m;e, this cousin Jeanne must indeed be fair if she resembles you! You will say to the Vicomte that he must not be selfish. We will teach him that jewels are not bestowed to be shut up in a casket; they are meant to shed their lustre around, and gladden the eyes that behold Ahem. Sweet friend, you will tell this gentleman that his young Countess Jeanne must be placed in your keeping .at Amboise,"
Once more the beautiful woman thandked her Royal lover with the languid grace that was one of her greatest charms in the eyes of the amorout monarch.
When Francis had quitted the chamber, Madame de Chateaubriand touched a small bell on the table beside her couch.
"Tell the Vicomte d'Orbec I will see him," she said to the attendant who appeared.

Soon after the man returned, ushering in Rolland de la Touche. He looked pale, for he had only lately recovered from the effects of his wound. Fortunately, Laval's dagger, instead of piercing the flank, had buried itself in the muscles near the hip-bone, so that recovery had been rapid.

Rolland bowed low. But Madame de Chateau- briand smiled sweetly and held out her hand. He bent over the white fingers, and kissed them with a reverence that surprised himself. The strong likeness to Jeanne in those limpid grey eyes and exquisite complexion, framed by rich auburn hair, made him forget, for the momen+, the prejudice he had cherished against her frail cousin, Feaneoise de Foix. "I rejoice, monsieur, to see "—her voice sounded caressing in its soft, persuasive tones—"that yea have recovered from the wound you received at St. Bonnet. I owe you gratitude. You look surprised, monsieur. My young cousin told me how, at the risk of your life, you saved her from the snares of a villain." I did but the duty of a brother to a sister, madame, for in her father's Castle of Longuedec Jeanne Kergrist and I grew up like sister and• brother." Madame de Chateaubriand smiled. "I know, I know, but not quite a sister, Monsieur; the sweet child told me all her story, and her blushes told me that she had changed brother into lover. Eh, Monsieur le Vicomte? " He thought she was lovelier than ever as a sparkle of mischief shewed in her sweet grey eyes. "Pardon me, madame, but I did not know you had seen her," "Years ago, in my Breton home "—he heard a slight catch in the soft voice—"my cousin, Jeanne's mother, was like an elder sister to me." She paused an instant. "I must now requite my cousin's kind- ness. While Jeanne and her trusty Gillonne were nursing you at St. Bonnet, the dear child wrote and asked my counsel about her future movements, for she knew that she was a Ward of the King. I had been summoned to Lyons, and I bade Jeanne meet me on my way thither. In the short time she spent with me—for she was impatient to return to you—l saw that she was truly her mother's daughter. Now listen, my lord. The King gives you leave to wed Jeanne de Laval, who has, with his Majesty's permission, returned to her old home. He also gives you leave to quit the army for six months, so that you may —she (smiled archly—"set your estates in order, and ley at least thirty lances to accompany you to Italy. ' "Madame, how can I thank you, and his Majesty ? " "Stay, monsieur," the favourite continued; "I claim my share in Jeanne; when you quit your sweet wife, she must come to me at Amboise. You agree to this? " She put up her lips in pretty, pouting entreaty, but Rollancns eyes remained fixed on the ground. There was silence, save for the buzzing of a fly against the lattice. At first a little vexed flush rose on Madame de Chateaubriand's face, the vexation of a spoilt beauty, whose will is law to those around her. But as the silence lasted she grew pale, then a deep rosy colour spread over face and throat, show- ing vividly against the white fur bordering of her bodice._ _ _ .

"Madame," he said at last, in a firm yet respect- ,t tone, "you must pardon me if I ask whether :JCAI consider Amboise a good home for a fair young rife, in her husband's absence ? " Ire looked up; her face was hidden between her hands, and he saw bright tears falling between her slender fingers. Rresently she spoke her voice was low and trembling. "Monsieur, you are right Keen your Jeanne

away from the dangers of the Court." She held out her hand. "Adieu! Greet your love for mei and bid her make you happy—happy as you deserve to be." Rolland bowed over the beautiful hand, ape kissed it.

S.apence a fistful is the pries, and although the fi-hee are generally smakit is much Cheaper than purchasing by weight. ffobody, of Course, can hold eels in the naked hand. She was picked up unconscious, an I died on her way to her home. whither she was conveyed in a cab. Coventry. one of tho ofa 'era who took part in the Jameson raid, sailed from the NI orsey on Saturday for Akassa, on what is believed obe special Government service connected with the raising and training of native levies in the neighbourhood of Bonin. A destructive re ocaurred at Middlesborough on Tuesday, the extensive timber yard and saw mills of Messrs. Hallam and Sons being completely destroyed. The oil and bonded stores adjoining the sawmills narrowly escaped becoming a prey to the flames. As it is the damage will be very large. The floor of a building in Govan-road,Goven near Glasgow, collapsed on Monday afternoon, and crashed through into a grocer's shop below Five men at work on the building were killed, and three other persons were injured. The assistants in the grocer's shop were, with one exception, uninjured. At the Old Bailey on Monday, John Payne was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour and twenty strokes with the eat for highway robbery with violence. Charles Silk WAS also sentenced to three years' penal servitude and twenty strokes with the cat for highway robbery with violence in Clerkenwell.

Shortly before eight is'elock on Monday night fire broke out in Millwall Docks, London, and within art hour and a half buildings stored with valuable merchandise, and cover- ing several acres of ground, had become involved. During the night fire engines from all parts of London were pouring water on the flames.

Annie Clifford, aged twenty-two, a maz rie:l woman, work- ing as a polisher at Birmingham. tock a lamp up3tairs, and. baring undressed, blew down the chimney. An explosion took place, as the result of which she suffered t.rrible burns. She died from the shock a few hours after her admission to the Queen's Hospital.

The raped that two Italian anarchists had planned an attempt on the life of the Italian Crown Prince in Syria during his journey to Vienna to attend the Empress's funeral. is denied from Vienna, but it is admitted that in conseqnence of certain rumours a strict, watch was kept on his Royal Highness's line of route. Herbert Plnnington, of Peckham, while riding a brakeless bicycle down a steep hill near Westerham, Rent, on Satur- day, lost control of the machine, and, failing to round a corner, dashed with t,rrific force into the bank. His held was fractured against a tree, and after lingering a couple of hours at the neighbouring parish-room, lie died.

At an adjourned inquest, held at Seafo th on Monday Peter and Mary Brady, 11, Catherine-terrace, Litherland, were on the coroner's warrant committed to the assizes for trial on a charge of manslaughter, the jury returning, a verdict that their two yew old child, John Patrick Brady, died from starvation, brought on by culpable negligence °a the part of both parents.

On 'Monday morning, Mrs. Brame Harding. residing at Brownlow Mews, Holborn. was carrying a lighte i paraffin lamp upstairs when It exolorled. Hr husb snd went to her assistance, but both were so terribly burnt that they had to be couveyed to the Royal Free Hospital, where the woman died during the afternoon from the effects of burns and shook to the system. Nawab Akbar 'Khan. otherwise William Davies" was on Tuesday convicted at the Old Bailey of stealing a paper-knife belonging to Lord Balfour of Burleigh, and sentenced to eignteen months' hard labour. The prisoner was an impostor of some ingenuity, and his victims included quite a number of prominent personages. He is said to have lived on the proceeds of his frauds for sixteen years. On Monday morning a crowded electric car Ore the Great Horton tramway line, Bradford, failed to turn a sh ,rp Curve at the bottom of a steep gradient. wee overturned against a wall, and completely wrecked. The driver and conductor and many of the passengers were injured, severil of the latter soseriously that one has since died, and three others are regarded as in a critical condition. On Saturday, Mr. J. B. Smallwood, a prominent member of Over, Oheshire.Cycling Club. met with a serious accident. He was cycling with a companion down a steep hill at West- gate. near Northwich when a restive horse belonging to the Earl of Ruaiskillen, which was being exercised by a groam, swerved into him, He was pitched violently across the read, was badly bruised and shaken, and both hands were severely cart. •

While two brothers named Harvey, with a companion named ileymer, were bathing at Yarmouth on Saturday. thev got out of heir depth. William Adams, a bathing Imachine proprietor, went to their assistance, and succeeded n bringing one of the Harveys and Itevose- vhore. Adams dived for the other Harvey, ald brought the boy to the beach, but efforts to restore life were unavailing. Deceased belonged to Gorleston. A young man named Pope, aged nineteen, who was in the employ of Mrs. Preicott•Westeir. of the Herne Bay Model Dairy, met with his death under sad circumstances. With two companions he went out to bathe from a boat After a time his two companions re entered the boat, and while they were dressing Pope was seen etrugg,linst in the water. Before assistance could be rendered the unfortunate young man sank In ten feet of water, and his body was not recovered until later in the day. An interesting Blue book on the railway accidents in 1897 has been issued by the Board of Trade. The number of per- sons killed in train accidents is stated to have been eighteen, and 324 were Injured. in the previous year the numbers were five and 388 respectively. There were 1,165 persons killed and 6,102 injured, from all Causes, in the working of railways, 133 of the killed being passengers and 510 servants of companies or contractors. There were also 90 persons killed and 11,274 injured by accidents which were not con- nected with the movement of railway vehicles. Thus the personal accidents reported during the year brought up the totals to 1,255 persons killed and 17.378 injured.

JUBILEE OF :it YCLIFFE CONGREGx- TIONAL CEIIIRCET, WA.RRINGTON.
INTERESTING 13ISTORICAL FACTS.

Ilarv( st thanksgiving services were held in Wycl:ffe Ceneregetmeal Church on Sunday, and at tic eveairee ser eice occa-den was taken by the Past or to refer te the Jubilee of the church Within the co nmueion rails a theice selectien of flewers and plant, had been taste • fully arrang d, ail they tookel partivarlv ate-ac•eve. The musical portion ef the :vertices had received seecial attention. The anth-m "0 Lord how inenifolcr (learn- t 5; was sung by the choir at the mrniig service, end at night two anthems were sung "Lighten our da• k less" ((1. R. Vicars), and " Let the peeple praiie Thee" (W. 11. Payton). 'Nis Was the first time the anthem c rn- poe"d by Mr. W. H. Payton MM. Sac., the respected organist of Wycliffe Church, had been sung, and it was favourably commented upon. It contains some very fine passages both for the soloist atti choir, and is very appropriate for hervest thanksgiving servic Mrs. R. H. Pearson gave an effective rendering of the solo part. The sermee was preached by the Rev. John Yonge. He took for his text the words" He thanked God and took courage," Acts 28 chapter, 15 verse Aftar referring to the experiences of Paul which lei him te ex- press himself in the words of the tett he acid the words seemed to suggest What sheuld be their duty that night as belonging to Wycliffe. The words did not specially connect themssivits, indeed, with the idea of haresst thanksgiving. •Incidently and inclusively,however,they might find even that connection. But this season with teem at Wycliffe had additional fi a'u-es of in•erest be- yond t',at of harvest. This was the Jubilee year,tee 50th year of the existence of the religious community in the , town which had been known und,,r the noble historic name of Wycliffe. It was in 1848, that a movement wa 4 made und ir the auspices of the Lancashire Congre- gational Union, to revive the Congregational i sterest in Warrington. From a variety of c eises, in o which they need net now enquire, th it interest had through many previous years been only in a languishing condition. " Independennye as it used formerly to hes called, took its rise in this town ee far back as 1779-120 years ago. In consequence of the preaching ot Unitstian doctrines at Cairo-street, a por- tion of the congregation withdrew and erected what was known as Stepney Ceapel in King-street. Subseq lently in 1811, Salem C 'ape! in Golbarne-street, now beld by the Baptist Church, was built in consequence of a dis- agreement in the Stepney Society, and a runtime of the original Stepney people worshipped there for many years. This division of interest was detrimeital to the Congregational cause, an lied the way to its dc idence and doctrine. When, however, in the end of 1817 and beginning of 1818, the Lancashire Congregational Ueion began services in the large Assembly Room at the Nag's Head in Sankey-street, Congregationalism began to slowly re-assert itself, and from that date to make -steady progress. There were, of ourse, S^ll3B Still am )ne them who could recall those days of 50 years ago—although only quite rivently, not a few of those adherents had paesed away. It WAS in- teres'inz to know that the Congregational revival in Warrington was greatly helped and guide hi sli'3l3 notable Congregational leaders as the late Dr. Vaughan, 'hen princmel of Lancash're College ; Dr. Halley, then pastor of Cavendish Ceurch, Manchester; Dr Raffles and the Rev. Johe Kelly, the two Congreeational pas- tors of that day in the city of Liverpool. TtleS4 were the men who brought about the better day, and it wacas the issue el their work, begun 50 years ago, that the first Wycliffe Chapel was erected. That place of worship Was opened in 1851— the opening service be- ing conducted by tome of the ministers jest named, and ateo by the celebrated John , Angell Jame'. of Birmingham. The first feaster was the Rev. P. A. Hampeon, who was fillowel in 1853 by tee Rev John Kay, who resigned rather more than two years ' later. Then there was an interval of 18 months when the pulpit was" vacant " as they usually said—that was here was no settled minister ; but in February,lBs7 the Rev. C. E. Palmer became the paator,conlinuing as such for 18 month., u 'tit July 1858 when he retired. He was followed in February, 1859 by the Rev. Richard Jeeem who con' inland his ministry until June 1868 and deol in 1859. It nat during the pastorate of Mr. Jessop that more room was receeired far Sunday School work. That had been carried on for some time in the transept of the chapel, but in 1865 an additional plot of land was taken,and some of the scheol buildings which they had to day were erected. In September, 1868 the pastorate of the church was taken by the Rev. George Sale Reaney —preleusle a Baptist minister, but who oe accepting Peed -Baptist views,eetered the Congregational ministry es pester of Wycliffe Church. Now the time of Mr. Heaney's residence and work there must ever remain upon the record of the church as a period of re- markable progress and growth. Successive enlarge- ments of the chapel and schools took place, and the Wycliffe cause grew and extended very rapidly. Much of this Was doubtless due to Mr. Reaney's energy, fresh. ! nese, fertility of resource. personal attractiveeese. But the success of a church was never only due to the minister. His usefuiness greatly depended upon whose woo ere his co-workers. Hence it was only just to say that Mr. Reaney was seconded and supported in his day by a company of leaders such as ha I it in their power with God's blessing, to lead any relieims movement to a good success. The pragress and success of Wycliffe were largely due to the character and consecrated en- rgy and devoted services of Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Rigby, Mr. and Mrs. R. W. Murray, as well as Mr. ant Mrs. Zile I Armitage who still were and they trusted ler long years would yet continue to be, with them. The church also received generous financial support in those days not only from those already named but also from the late Mr. McMinnies, who always displayed de le interest in and strong attachment to Wycliffe , And besides these, there were other earnest Workers—one almost feared to name any lest some whos , work was noteworthy should be overlooked ; hue toe names and faces came to him as he looked back of men and women whom he found when became there in 1876 but who now had been withdrawn, either by local removal or death itself, e.g. James Stelfox,John Mennen, William Walineton, Richard Roberts, Mre.Brinsley,Miss Rigby, Miss Garnett, Mrs. Tunstall, Mrs. Percival, miss Garner, Frederick Knott, who did such true service in the Sunday School,and many more. These, all or most, were linked with Mr. Ramey in his work, and helped , along with him the expansion of Wycliffe in the years 1868 to 1873. In 1871 the first Wycliffe chapel being found toe small was demolished. The congregation then assembled in the Pubic Rail, until September 4, 1873, when the present building was opened for worship. The premises cost a suns of £9,000, or thereabouts, as he gathered from the published accounts, including the cost of the splendid organ which had been so noble an aid to the music of that sanctuary. It must have been indeed a memorable day for all concerted when this work was achieved I It was achieved as the result of some very noble generosity on the part not only of the richer but also of the poorer constituents of the com- munity. As long as the building stood it would be a monument to the faith, courage, and heaeficence of the men and women of 25 years ago. He did not think it at all invidious, but simply a statement of fact, to say th it to Mr. Samuel Rigby and his devoted wire, more than to any others, Congregationalism in Warrington Was in- debted. Both were now long since passed away ; but to the day of their death they loved tnose walls and that cause. And the now proposed memorial to their honour —"better late than never"—was in his judgment riehl v and thoroughly deserved. In the year 1876, Mr. Reaney resigned hie pastorate and re- moved to Reading. He (Mr. Yonge) WRS his immediate sumessor, and by the goodness of Gd and their good will he continued " unto this day." It was hardly for him to attempt any review of the 22 years that had nearly expired. So much, however, might be said. They had been years of useful, and in many ways, happy service. Their good results were discern- able to some degree in the substantial increase of the Church fellowship • in the fair maintenance of their numerical standard ; considering the many new or revived interests in town, the removal of many familim to the suburbs, which hindered their regular attenealee as in the days of their town residence. They had wit- nessed considerable changes. Death had carried away many who had been active and conspicuous. They did not now posse's the same financial resources that were once available. But they could not mnet there that night and make honest review of the history of that Church, from the time of its renewal in 1848, and mere still from the date of its entrance upon the bitied- ing without feeling moved to profoundly " thank God." There had been rich" times of refreshing." There had been lives uplifted and ennobled. There had been sad hearts comforted. There had been souls guided into peace. There hal been true work done for the Master. In sanctuary worship, in church ordinance, in school labour, in missionary enterprise, in endeavour to benefit workiae men, Wycliffe Church had been made a bless- ing, and on that anniversary day they would " thank God." And should not the emotion of gratitude awakened and deepened by the sense of mercy past,cen- firmed by the tokens by no means lacking of mercy prc• sent,inspire them to take courage"for the future"? Yea ! verilf I! What they needed was to seek and obtain a renewal of spiritual rower and zeal. They needed to open heart and mini afresh to the spirit of Jesus. They could not uphold that Church or pulpit and spiri- tual work with their own strength. No Church could be run upon the principles and methods of the world. RI must be distinguished and guided by the word and wil of the Master. If they surrendered to that ;if they yielded themselves to Him ; if they sought His Glory first and most, they would see greater things teal had ever been seen before, and should do greater things. They were now as they were aware projecting an enter- prise at Wycliffe that called for activity, industry, gen- erosity, and perssverance. It could only be done well if done unitedly, cordially. Younger and older should enter into mutual and cordial compact. There should be a bravo rallying of the forces —not to fight—not to fight a foe save indirectly now : but to do a great work that might equip them to fight better in years ahead. Let them" Thank Gad and take courage I" He concluded with an earnest appeal for help. They must thank God for the many blessings they had received. They must go on in the strength of the Wycliffe motto graven on the foundation stone, "If God I be for us, who can be against us !"

FACTORY PROSECUTION AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Fri- day, before the Mayor (Alderman Wright) and other magistrates, Joseph Bernard, " The Laundry." Wiiderspool, was summoned at the instance of Mary Muirhead Paterson, Inspector of Fac- tories, for employing the following girls longer than allowed by law, in July last, namely :—Sliza- beth Pinnington, Esther Dainteth, Annie Lamb, Annie Ashurst, and Mary Wardle. Miss Paterson read section 22 of the Act of 1895.—Ar. Uasworth represented the defendant. The regulations, Miss Paterson said, differed from other regulations governing factories. Young persons were not to work in laundries more than twelve hours a day and women fourteen hours, or sixty hours per waek. She would prove that the weekly hours had been much in eXCess.

Elizabeth Pennington, 15 years of age, said that on Alonday, July 11th, she went to work at 9 a.m. and left off at 8 p.m. The next day she went at 7 a.m. and ceased work at 8 p.m. On the Wednesday and Thursday she worked the same hours, and on the Friday and Saturday from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. She was allowed quarter of an hour for breakfast, an hour flr dinner, and half an hour for tea.—By Mr. un4worth : Sometimes they would be at the works, but would not commence work till nearly eight o'clock. , Miss Paterson said that if a person was on the I ' premises according to the Act she counted as be- ing at work. They had exceeded the limit in this case by seven hours. She added that the firm which owned numerous laundries had been speci- ally instructed in the matter this year, and she asked that a substantial penalty be inflicted, Mr. Unsworth said although the girls might be on the premises at 7 o'clock they did not start work till 7.30 and 7.45. In that case the amount of o overtime was only three hours 11e had advised exception person of that and against in ost n Mary Wardle, Wardle, to the his client to plead guilty in regard to all the cases s whowith wt hae,a young same regulations as the girls in the other cases. Mary Wardle was then called by Miss Paterson and stated that on Saturday July 16th she worked from five a.m, until 10.15 P.m—By Mr. Unsworth : She came at five a.m. at her own request, because she wanted a holiday on the following Monday. She made from 275. to 325. per week. The Inspector stated tha:-. the hours in Wardle's case were exceeded by four. Mr.Unsworth speakinglon behalf of the defendant said the ' hours worked in one week were 73. The time for their meals (81 hours) would re- duce the figures to 64i hours. Ile submitted that there was a slight excess, but it was in the busiest month of the year. They earned good wages, and for that month it was not a great hardship to them It was only a technical breach of the Act, and it was a case in which the defendant ought to be dealt with leniently. Dr. Gornall thought it was the duty of the magis- trates to protect the employes and carry out the law. It was a very serious case. Alderman B.arrimon said the magistrates had a little latitude and he suggested that they ought to consider whether this was not a case in which that latitude ought to be extended.
Defendant,who was liable to a line of £lO in each case. was fined ss. and costs (19s. Bd.) in each case, .£4 17s. 61. in all,

WORK, WAGES, AND POLITICS. Ott Monday evening there waa only a far attendance at Cairo-st.echool to hear the lecturer Mr. Bruce Gluier en the Om subject. The chair was occupied ty Mr. J. Ball.

In introducing his subject the lecturer said although the titles might seem very practical to working men, they were bound to perceive fro:n experience during many years, that there was probably no subject in which working men seemed less jut nested, than in work and wages, and the formation of their aesociation Wag due more to thonghtful men than to working men. There were houses in London where at times men were gathered together, who representel all that literature, arts, and the sciences could realise, and yet within a few hundred yards of such houses there would probably be alums where people were starving for the common necessariel of life. If one was to ask a working man why he worked, the question would probably convey no meaning to him, though he would say .4 to earn his bread." The reply would be a very unsatiefactor e one. In many of the South Sea Islands they would find conditions of each a kind that neither man nor woman need toil—as they understood toll:—to earn their living. some•josos these Islanders are visited by Enropeass and t Oxen away to work and to earn money which they would spend on things which they had before not felt the need of. If they were askel why they worked,they would probably answer be ;aim they were compelled. If the working class were asked why they worked for the rich people they would be forced to admit that it was because they were compelled to work. This compulsion was due to i the fact that the rich had n their possession the means s. land and capital. All that the working man got for working was what the masters could be compelled to give. I The miner producing three or four tons of coal per day, would get less wages if he was able to produle thou- rands. The more work a man was able to produce, and the less value his work would have. He (the speaker) had formerly been a designer and had goed hours and wages. While at work in his OffiC3 he could see men working who had to get up early to go to their work and who looked out aexiously for the day to clone, yet at the week end they would ouly earn a third of the wages he did. Some peoVe thoieht that Socialists were men who were discontented and lied failed. It was not so. There was no escape from the fact that there would be more i difficulty in obtaining work n the future than there had been in the past. In many of the factories which a few years ago employed skilled labourers, machinery had now taken its place. There was no proposal made at the present day, by any responsible statesman which would mike any radical chanees. Insteacl,the competition with foreign labour almost was Morels. ing, and our colonies:were cemprting with tp in every line. Canada was threatening our English farmers. Our manufacturers were erecting mills in Inlja, and in view of the extraordinary introduction of machinery workmen would be entirely superseded. It was a gags. tion which politicians die not face. He pointed out that the best thing for the social salvation of the people was that everything should be for the community. To use the means of production for the whole of the natter' and so found a commonwealth. The water supply and public libraries were all equally divided amongst the community. Sanitary arrangements, fire brigades, etc., all those were for the good of the community. The lecturer concluded by pointing out in detail how badly labour was represented against capital.

for detaining him any longer. The C ironer : Before he was discharged he was taken before the committeo of visiting justices.—WitnesS : Decidedly. He was interviewed every day by the assistant medical officer and Dr. Wiggles. worth, and was finally examined by the Committee He was wired the USUiI questions as to whether he wanted to co out and if be had any complaints. He expressed himself as perfectly satisfied, and was anxious to bi discharged—The Coroner : As I under- stand, the asylum offi 2i oh take the full responsibility of ' the discharge P—Witness : The Medical Superintend= is almost boun It. The c ornmittee are guided by his. —The Coroner : Dr. Wieglesworth thought tile was a, case for discharge P—Witness : That is so. Even after a very long experience of these cases we cannot always tell. Of course it was unfortunate that the friends did ' not call in a constable or a reliefine officer when they , saw he was not well, but one c mid hardly blame them. Perhaps no one without a special knowled;e would have done so.—The Coroner : Is it not a fact that at th 3 present time the asylum accom- modation in Lancashire is quite inadequate for the cases which are continually arising Witness: I believi so, but it is not tbe case at RainhilL —The Coroner : We read in the newspapers that theta is a great conflict going on between Boards of Guardian and the Asylum Baard as to the accommodation provided hr lunatics. Has that any bearing in this case ? Do you try to make accommodation for dangerous cases by discharging milder ones, which otherwise you would keep P—Witness : I was n2t so in this case. I will not &ny it is so elsewhere, but as a matter of fact there is no such pressure at Rainfall!: The Coroner : And the man was not discharged on that acceuct P—Witness : Not at all. The symptoms he was seff.tring from on entering the asylum quickly subsided, and inieed completely disappeared after a we k. During the next three weeks he was quiet. bright, aid cheerful, and worked about the grounds of the inatitutioa. He could assure the Coroner that the man was perfectly well when he received his discharge. He must have undergone a mental relapse after leaving the asylum. The was nothing unusual in that. div.head: TRAGIC SUICIDE OF A JOINEtt.
div.p: THE TRAGIC SUICIDE OF A JOINEtt.
ADJOURNED INQUEST AND VERDICT.
TEIE SANICY OF THE DECEASED.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, resumed the inquiry at the Police Station on Friday morning, concerning the death of Thomas Brawn, who committed suicide at his motherie house, in Bank-street, on August 30th. The in- quest was opened a fortnight ago, when evidence was given to the effect that deceased was dischareed from the asylum at Hainhill on Monday, and committed suicide the following day. The relatives and the Coroner not being aatisfiel with the discharge as it then appeared on the evidence the inquiry was adjourned so that an official from the asylum could attend. Tee Coroner explained that the deceased had been in the asylum about a month,and atter his discharge appeared depressed and morose. On the 27th the mother of de- ceased received the following letter from the asylum : The Superintendent b-gs to inform Mrs. Brown that Thomas Brown has recovered, and has received his dis- charge from the asylum. It is necessary that he should be removed at once,and the Superintendent will be glad if Mrs. Brown will come or send for him as aeon as poes,ble He will require a complete outfit of clothes." The mother went en 'ha Monday and brought deceased home. The whole of the evidence gent to show that during his journeyeand when he arrived henne,deceased's condition was, if anything, worse than when he went to the asylem,a month previously. In other words, all the family said that in their opinion—and they were entitled to take it as corrent—he was worse that when he went. That being so he and the jet'c t ioug,ht —and very pro- perly—that the asylum autherities should be called upen to explain why they sent word that the man had recovered. On the face of it, it looked then, and still looked in the abseil%) of any explanation, that the man had been discharged improperly, and if he had been kept in his life might possibly have been saved. Peter Makin 41, Bank-street, said deceased was his stepson. He suffered from delusions, and six weeks ago gave himself up to the pelics a-id was afterwards taken to the Rainhill Asylum. On the Sa'urday before that they had a very rough night with him He thought that someone was in tee house, and after him. Before that he had at times seemed a little hit strange in his , manner. The letter ref errine to his discharge frem the I asylum was received on the 27th August, and was for- warded to deceased's wife, who was at Halton. She re- turned it,asking them to attend to the matter. Witness's wife and dee,eaaerl's brother William went to the asylum on Monday the 29 th,and brought deceased home in a trap. He (witness) saw the deceased at six in the evening. He looked very strang,,in fact he looked wilder in his eyes than when he went t the asylum. He also seemed to be very depressed ; he had hardly a word to say. So far as witness was able to judge, he had not recovered. He (witnesi) said to his wife, " Tom seems to be worse than when he went." Deceased went with his brother for a walk, but he said he felt very bad, and turned back home. He said that someone had him under observation. On Tuesday morning he seemed very low , and depressed. He said he would go back to the asylum ; he d'd not think he was safe, and would go and surrender himself on the Wednesday morning. Witness last saw him alive about four o'clock in the afternoon. From the time of his arrival home t 3 that time he had shown no signs of improvement. He was very wild and rough when he went to the asylum, but when he came back he was very low-spirited. He hardly seemed up to anything.—Dr. Menzies, acting medical superintendent at the Rainhill Asylum, who was present in the absence of Dr. Wigglesworth, sal I he had no questions to put to the witness. William Brown, brother of deceased, said he saw him on Sat erday and Sunday before he went away. He also went with his mother t 3 brine deceased home. When they got to the asylum his mother sew the doctor. When deceased came to him witness said " Well, Tom, how have you been going on ?" He replied "It has been a leseen to me ; wait until we get out." On the way home deceased only spoke when he was queationed. HA was very quiet. Before he had been in the house half an hour witness could see he was not right. A general opinion was formed by the members of the family that he had not recovered. During the night he went worse. About two o'clock he came int" the room where witness was sleeping and said •• Bill, light the gas there is someone in the house." Witness lighted the gas, and deceased remained in his room during the night. He did not see much of him on the Tuesday, but in the evening he saw him in the street and asked him where he was going. He said he was going to Joe Welsby's. Witness said "You have no tools," and deceased replied that he could borrow some. When he got to the bottom of the street he said he thought he would not go. They both had a chink of herb beer. Deaeaaed afterwards said. " yoo might be surprised if I went back." Witness asked where, and he said " Rainhill." Witness said if be was comfortable there he might as well. Deceased said " I am under observation. You may not think so, but I knew I am." The Coroner: It was quite clear he had not recovered from his delusions. —Witness: I said it would be better if he went hack. Laura Brown, wife of deceased, said the last time sh. saw him alive was the day before he went to Rainhill He was then at the Workhouee. He was very much surprised to see her, and said he thought She had been murdered. He told the doctor in witnesses presence that three men were trying to murder him on Saturday night. He promised three men in the Workhouse 103. each if they would assist him to escape. He was afraid to eat his food because he thouzht it had been drugged. Witness did not see him again. She was in service and away. She was coming to Warrington to see him the day after he committed suicide. She thought it was a great mistake for hies to have been discharged in so short a time. His father was an inmate of the asylum for 14 years. The dereased was 29 years of age the day he was diFchargsd. Dr. Menzies said deceased was admitted to the asylum on the 4th nit., suffering from slight melancholia and delusions, among them those which his wife had men- tioned. He showed no suicidal tendency during the time he was at the asylum, and he was comfortable and happy and thought he was going on all right. By the end of the week his delusions had entirely subsided— that was to say, he slept well, ate well, and talked with the attendants and medical officer. Be said his delu- sions had simply been caused be drink,and Le would not think any more of them. For the there following weeks he remained perfectly free from any symptoms of insanity, and accordingly he was discharged by the committee en the 26th. Witness agreed with the evidence of the friends, that he had had a relapse, when he found he bad to face the world again. That was a perfectly reasonable and rational explanation, and the unfortunate part was that no one could foresee it. It only occurred in a minute percentage of cases, but it in I occur. They knew that such relapses came on with great suddenness. Seeing the outsith world, golne back home might bring on a towards euicide. The explanation he sudden(witness) n gaveapu ls °was that it was a hereditary alcoholic .d deceased tecweoaUseldd "se. His fatql4ueritdeieidllefgroaml taolcohhaovliec indseatnaiitnye asylum any longer when he had hinavethb(loon been free from symptoms for three weeks They were not justified in detaining a man who had entirely lost his delusions. They were quite willing to stretch the elasticity of the law in cases where slight symptoms remained, but deceased was entirely free from ahem, an ithere was no provieion in the Lunacy Acts
