div.head: E EX A. AI N E •
div.p: E EX A. AI N E •
SEPTEMBER 23rd, 189 S.

1 THE Concert of Europe is A Blunt Instrament 1 and a Sharp One. very much like the coulter of a plough—excellent to tear up the earth if pulled through it, but useless to fell timber or shava with. Just now the pro- cess required in Crete is not what can be done by a coulter. The SULTAN has no fear of the Concert, because he knows what a blunt instrument it is, and he has had experience:.before of its ineffective- ness. If the Powers are to agree •to a common policy they must consult and empower one of their number to act. Otherwise, there will be very little accomplished, rho SULTAN is much too clever to be coerced ley a joint body which has private as well as public aims. He has shown us before that he can succeed in paralysing action most effectually, and he hopes to do it again. The idea was to give the British authori- ties in Crete as much trouble as possible, and then to employ the Concert to blunt the action of Great Britain, enjoying our confusion in private. But Admiral Nom. is not a coulter—he jean axe. The SULTAN does not like him at all. He has begun to oppose him in a varietylof ways,through EDHEM PASHA, through DJEVAD PASHA, and throwh the other Powers, se far as they can be influenced against us. The opposition seems likely to be in vain. The new policy is of a bold character, and naturally the SULTAN is alarmed. He is not in. I dined to admire bluff British Admirals and posi- tive ways of doing ,things. The grievances affect the honour and position of this country as one of the interested Powers. The VICE-CONSUL at Candia has been murdered,and British soldiers and seamen have been killed by armed Bashis, under the eyes of a Turkish coramander,who had regular troops in his control, and who could have stopped the rioting if he pleased. Our p ilicy now is to obtain collective sanction to individual action. Admiral NOEL has compelled the surrender of some of the ringleaders of the riot. Hs may not have the 1 right men, and he may not have the whole of them but he has got some of them. He is proceeding to disarm the Bashis, and the work is going on. He will then, we hope, have obtained the assent of the Powers or act without it in demanding the exit of Ihe Tarkish troops. Ha has assured the Cretan Christians that he does not want their help and that he will not permit them to attack the Candi- otes or the Bashis. He clearly means to use a Sharp instrument, and to make an end of a busi- ness that becomes dangerous by delay, and can only be settled by oae power. The SULTAN fears the action of England alone more than anything else, because he knows he cannot resist it, and can- not send a vessel to Crate with reinforcemen ts whilst we command the sea. The policy of giving in always angers the Ottoman Turk, and he loaves lt to the last moment. Hap?ily, in Admiral NOEL we have a man who has a short and effectual way with dodging and procrastinating officials.

T HE effect of suggestion on the Train criminal mind is well known. wreckers. The influence of events on the imagination of the weak-minded who are not criminal is also known. Offences against person and property are apt to follow in a sequence to which we can give no other title than that of an epidemic. Judges have often had occasion t,) call attention to the repetition of definite crimes. We speak of an epidemic of garrotting, criminal assaults on women and children, and even of mur- der and suicide. We are quite warranted in so doing. No other explanation is possible. Jus ZIONV there are indications that a new form of Crime is being attempted due to what we may

call suggestion. No train has been actually' wrecked by obstructions placed on the line, but there have been so many attempts in different parts of the country that we can only explain them by the assumption that criminal and weak ' minds have been influenced by reacting of the at- tempts made, and have been stimulated to imita- tion. On the Midland, on the London and North-Western, and now on the South Western there have been attempts of this dastardly,di boli- cal character. It is inconceivable that they are the result of any regular conspiracy. At least, there is no evidence to warrant that belief. They seem to be individual, prompted by weak-mindedness and cruelty.

In the public interest these attempts call for the most active vigilance. The Companies which , have been already attacked are taking great pre- cautions at likely places, and it is clear that, with : Gut wishing to unduly alarm travellers, the rail- way companies will be wise to guard the more. danprous places and to be on the look-out forf loafets. The prJbability seems to be that the- • , wretch who has made several efforts to wreck 1 trains is is custody. He is probaby insane, with a method in his madness. What would be most ; ,salutary, however, would be to catch one of theseS miscreants red-handed, and to hand him over to, the police at once. The summary punishment of such a dastard might have as wholesome all '- effect on the imaginations of the weak and the criminal as the accounts of former wrecking efforts have had in the other direction. Train-wrecking is such a horrible business that no punishment can been too severe for any person found engaged in the work. Sending them to a criminal lunatic asylum if they are insane is,of course, the obvious thing to be done. But where there are no traces of mental weakness the "cat " and penal servitude seem to be very appropriate punishments. The eat is coming into favour again as a deterrent, and chiefly because ruffianism is getting so corn' men and mild measures produce so little deterrent effect on the imagination. We cannot think, however,that unless insanity be clearly established there will be any disposition to deal leniently with wretches who are ready to imperil the lives ana limbs of a train load of travellers.

It is eight years since the Channel Squadron visited Liverpool,and as a natural consequence the presence of a portion of the fleet in the Merseir throughout this weekend is an event of s ery con' siderable importance. Nearly all people,including those by nature the most pacific, feel a justifiable pride in Britain's unrivalled navy;and as a modern attleship is an instrument of the most fearful and wonderful description even to those of whom the sight of one is no novelty, it is not surprising that dwellers inland are looking forward with (Imp interest to the visit of four leviathan battleships and a gunboat. Events on sea and land during the past year have stimulated largeli the interest felt in the arm timents of nations, Se that all things combined the Channel Squadron certain to be well inspected during the course 01. to-day, Sunday, Monday,and Tuesday between the hours of 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. The fighting machines due at the port are the battleships Nile (flagshiP)t Trafalgar, Sanspariel, Thunderer,and the gun- eoo Spanker. The latter is newer than her big consort° though they are by no means antiquated and fairly be regarded as samples of the matert Britain's maritime supremacy is maintained wit No charge will be made for admission to vessels, and the Lancashire folk flocking in thei". thousands will only be called upon to expend,l/ modest shilling (the fare to and from the vessels?, over and above the expenditure necessitated travelling to Liverpool.

A scarcity of stores, medicines,Bl3. hospital accommodation proved fatal as an Or, demic.A New York paper has compiled some strikllllo statistics showing the causes of mortality during the war. Altogether the grand total °a deaths in which the Spaniards had active participation was 2086, while 40,000 tee.ri„ are reputed to be stricken by disease. SP01", might possibly have won in Cuba had the oil: dragged on through the rainy season, so well Ws' she assisted by sickness and tne unpreparedleo! of the American forces to cope with it. There er° bitter complaints in America at this waste of lifs!4 I and comparisons made with the healthiness so' effectiveness of the Campaigners under the Sad/ do not allay the grumbling. Mismanage rat seems to have been rife,and there can be no donu" of America's unreauiness for the war into which a- plunged.

Ritualism in its later phases is a move- tent, not a rebellion headed by leaders, a move- eaent goingßomewards, or even to a worse gaol, if 3'eu will, but most certainly not a revolt that can be stamped out by arbitrary unfrockings hero and there. Congregations that have been led into ritualism would still be ritualistic after the disap- Pea.rance of their clergymen, and would demand satisfaction. The Wise Colonel does not, in fact, provide a wise solution of this difficulty.

Queen's Gardens are now progressing towards et:flipletion at a speed which will be satisfactory everyone not inclined to be hypercritical. The c°Ping stones which were the cause of so much de- are now in position, and with the grass-plots 4'Bo laid order is beginning to evolve out of what ;vas, a short time ago, nothing but chaos. We eel bound to compliment those responsible on the rhdition of the grass. It has been beautifuilly id and the attention bestowed on it since is at °nee evident in the closeness, greenness,and fresh- of the surface. The unsightly brickbats are Lsappearing rapidly under their asphalt covering, a,a(l the walks now possess some resemblance to 'flair real character. But the principal event in ,eonnection with the laying out of the gardens is arrival of the fountain presented by Mr. R. arnett, J.P., and which is now installed in the Ilentre of the grounds. As it is intended for pub IC use it roust pass through the ordeal of criticism , We must confess to some slight feeling of dis- PPointment now that it has arrived. It is not a fountain in the accepted meaning of the word— that is, there is no stream of water ePrayed into the air. A more correct WaY of describing it would be to call it a , dritiking-fountain, which it is solely and simply. One of the first-mentioned sort,with thirst-quencq- lag facilities combined, would have been much %ore imposing and ornamental. Still the fact 1-Ist not be overlooked that Mr. Garnett volun- tarily offered to provide the fountain, and the People of Wairington should, and will, we doubt riot, feel grateful co him for so generously adding to the attractiveness and utility of Queen's Gar- dens. By the way, our jocular prophecy of a few months ago that they would be opened in Nov- ember simultaneously with the advent of winter's cold and dreary blasts seems likely to be fulfilled. It is a pity that the Gardens could not have been rendered accessible to the public at a much earlier slate. Such an oasis in the desert of streets and houses would have been indeed welcome during the past and prevailing hot weather.

The suicide, of Thomas Brown, a joiner, is !low proved to have been unpreventable. It will be remembered that at the Coroner's first enquiry facts were disclosed which demanded explanation, Ile it was adjourned till Friday last. The feature of tbe case was the question raised as to whether the teased, who had been an inmate of Rainhill Yluna was sufficiently cured of his mania to tllBtify his discharge. His relatives asserted that 6 was worse on arrival home than when he first iet,t to the institution, which appears to have „,eefl the case as he committed suicide within a :erY short time after his release. Seeing that the Illcrease of lunacy has somewhat overcrowded .111;t1)3, asylums, the ugly suggestion presented it- to one's mind that perhaps Brown had been Bent home, imperfectly cured, to make room for a tlre„wer and maybe more dangerous arrival. That Mr. tuoroner Brighouse had this in his mind, or when ne Ldjourned the inquest was evident by the 'enour of hisreinarks on Friday. Fortunately the Fxplatiation from the medical authorities of Rain- nAll clears away these unpleasant conjectures. thec°l-nrnodation for instance, is ample there, but o main point is the mental condition o', the deceased when discharged, The natements of both Dr. Wigglesorth and ipassistant medical officer leave no room for i„°lll3t that, as far as it was possible for anyone to lige,Brown was quite sane and ready to go when eased. The only reason they can give tor his °llbsequent awful deal is that his zoming once I:l',)re into contact with the busy world and his selatives, caused a sadden return of the mania. • tleb a thing could not have been foreseen though Ithhas been known to happen before. We think e friends and relatives of the poor fellow should 2w rest, or satisfied that everything possible was 1-I?rie to effect his return to sanity, and that no olame attaches to the medical staff of Rainhill S-sylum for his sudden relapse and its terrible sequel.

PAIN:UTE MEE IN TROUBLE.—GeMZO rt olcroft ,F r oder ick Trigger, and Thomas Morris, all of Padgate,were charged at Warrington County Potty Sessions on Wednesday with treripassing in search of game on certain laud at Woolston, in ths occupation of Jcp2eph Houghtun.—Mr.Browne,who appeared for too defendants, made a suggestion to the effect that the case should be adjourned, as there were no witnessrs for the defence, and a very valuable Act would come into force on October lst,which would enable tile defendants to give evideuca on their own behalf.—.. The magistrates decided to hear toe CARL—P.C. Bellinger said he was with P.C. Clarke at 5.30 on the morning in question, when they saw toe hree def,ndants on Mr. Houghton's tad. Trigs.:er and Holcroft each had a gun. They were about a hundred yards distant from one another, and Morris was is the centre. The men Lad a dog with them,and witness watched them for twenty minutes. He heard five shots previously,but did not see by whom they were fired.—Cruss-examined : He beard one shot while he was talking to defendants—P.C. Clarke and Sergeant Brindle also gave evidence.—Mr. Browne said defendants Trigger and Flolcroft hid per- mission to shoot on land adjoining Mr. lisughtin's,and hey denied they hal been on any other land. Morris had no gun, and in fact had only gone out to gathrr mushrooms. Defendants were lir spectable young men,and if the Bench considered the case proved he thought a small penalty would meet it.—Morris was ordercd to pay costs, and the other defendants were fined 10s.each.

div.p: BEFORE THE M ktitd CRA.CES
ATTEMPTING TO DEFRAUD TEN LONDON AND NORTE. WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

At the Borough Court on Friday William Stoekton, slmployed as " trot.; " at the Li tn Hotel, Bridee-st., was charged with travellieg on the London and North-Wes- tern Railway between Liverpool and Warrington with- out a ticket and with intent to avoid payment.—Mr. Fianna prosecute 1 on behalf of the Railway Company and Mr. Unswoith defende I.—ln opening the case Mr. Fenna stated that the e,sence of the charge was the intention to avoid payment. He thought they would see from the defendant's action and words at the time that he had na doubt as to what he had done. He arrival at Bank Quay (low level) station on the 14-th inst., by the 11 15 p.m. train from Lime-street station, Liverpool. At the outside door was collector Glover aesi--tecl on that tams sion by Detective Inspector Howells. The defendant on coming to the door was asked for his ticket by Howells. Be replied "I have given it up there" pointing to the platform. Howells then sent Glover with the de- fendant to see who the person was to whom be had given the ticket. The defendant failed to point him out and he was brought haek to How• 111. He then wanted to pay the fare from Lime-street bet Howells replied that he could not tak it as the defendant had tried to pass out without payment. Howells then took the de- fendant to his office with the object of getting his name and address. He gave his name but positively refused to give any address and used most abusive language. Be was taken 0 the Police Station and although a constable endeavoured to persuade him to give his address the defendant still refused. He was therefore left in custody of the police —Deteititre Howells then gave evidence bearing out the solicitor's statement. Prisoner told witness that he had a Cheshire Lines ticket, but bad given it up to a man in the train. Defendant said he was a &tech gP.—By Mr. Unsworth He appeared to be sober, and bof sre he left the station ' offered to pay his fare.—He ley Glover corroborated Mr. Patina's statement.—Mr. Unsworth said the prisoner was a respectable man, having been employed at the Hotel for twelve years. Prisoner said he gave his ticket up to someone when half asleep. He had had "a drop of drink." When he reached the exit gate he told the ticket collector he bad given his ticket up. He failed to find the man,and came back and wanted to par his fare (Is 61.). He had never been in trouble before, and he asked the magistrates to dismiss the case.—The Bench infl'eted a fine of 10s. and costes (£l. Os. 85.)

I must have been after the person who assaulted me, and beng drunk I did not I know who I struck —The Chief Cooatable said prisoner bad been in the army, had left, and was on Saturday soooin, to rejoin. Ookleston, Eliza Antrobas was charged with doing wilful damage to 17 panes of glass, of the value of 10s., at Dutton Work- Muse. She was Lather charged with misbehaviour at Dos Workboosse while an inmate of the place. Mrs. Cunnah, matron et the Workhouse, stated that the pri- soner h• d been in the house sines 1884. She had no parents, so far as witness knew. She had been before the Court prvinuslv far breaking winchwe, and Was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. On the present occa- sion the prisoner broke 17 windows in the day ward. She got op early and toll the inmates she was going to break 18 windows, so that she would get sent to prison. div.head: LA.NCASEIIRE SENIOR. COMPETITION. _- WAARINGTON v. ST. HELENS.
div.p: LA.NCASEIIRE SENIOR. COMPETITION. _- WAARINGTON v. ST. HELENS.
TEIS ROMRSTEati' FIRST WIN.

Warring,nn played the lest of their first instil- ment of noi.le matches on Saturday, when St. llelieve paid a visit to the Wilderspool grL and. The odds were certainly on the side of Warrington as they had a point better record than their visitors, and were able to disport themielves at home. Boa- cow resumed his place at full back, while a change was made in the tit ree.quarterline by substituting Duckworth for Hallam. The weather was by no means suited to fo)tball, though fine and dry, for the heat was most oppressive. There was a notice- able diminution in the sizs of the " gate," and 4,900 would cover the total adequately. Tile Saintiwere well represented and a fair contingent of spectators travelled Pout St. Helens by rail and road. The teams were composed as follow: _

Warrington: -Boscow, full bacic ; Moores, Isher- wood, Duckworth, and Holcroft, three-quarters • .1 T Bate and R. Bate, half backs Taylor, Deakin; Nsylor, Swift, Fairhurst, Boardman, Eden and Sud- low, forwards. _ _

• __ St.Heleas : Foulkes, full back; Barnes, Traynor, Flynn, and Si idall, three-quarters ; Briers and Boyle, half backs: Chapman, Glad win, Whitely, Thom peon, Taylor, Simpson, Dale, and Reynolds, forwards.

Tne Waerington skipper was again fortunate with the spin of the coin, and bad choice Of positions for the first, half of the game. St. Helens were thus caeed upnn to face the wind and ann. Traynor started and some ex- change kicking followed without afforeine advantage to either sde J. Bate and R. Bate got away from tee p ink and transferred to Eloicroft who put in a slice kick which was neutralised by a clever run from Traynor. Boyle and the latter coineinel well in a deals for the line but they were not allowed to go far. Poor kicking on the part of the visitors lost them ground and flelcroft rendered geol service to Warrington with a huge punt. The homeeters showed better form for a brietspell but all the advantags gained wee lost through a mistake 01 the part of the referee,and the Saints took up the attack. In f ward dribbling they were the superiors of War- rin.tton. end by a flee effort they got pest Boscow and applareri to have the line at their mercy woes Moores dashed up and dropped on ' the bill amid cheers of relief from the home crowd. Give and take play prevailed for some time,the principal item of ante benox a strong attack initiated by Tuber. wood and frustrated by Briers who 'saved under the posts in fine style. The Saints replied with another for- ward rush which nearly overcame Oho home defence, Holcroft coming to the rescue at a critical moment. A mis-kick by Boseow gave St. Helens a position in front of the home goal, where an easy chance to score wee nsiseed.by Flynn, Tne Saints were getting possession from the scurnmaesee, _and the borne line r eetnred a lot of defending. Btiftreenel Boyle were both held up Within art inch or tem of he line. At last the home captain relieved the teaslori by a judicious punt, and a moment later a passing movement between the Bates,Duck worth and Helernft remoied the danger entirely. Fairhurst made a couple of exceilent marks in succession which served tole's, St. Helens on the defence. The Saints made poer use of their opportunities,bad pulsing by the three/palters losing ground: .1. Bate gave • Holcroftee well judged pass and the wing man sped down the touch line at a great pace, only to be 'bowled over in the corner by Foulkes. Traynor navel capitally under the posts from Warrineten punts. Alter having several narrow escape I tee, visitors worked , their way back to centr a,where Ttayaor secured,only to , be grassed by Isherwood before he could get away'. 1 flolcroft had a •try at goal from centre but failed to raise the ball. Good play by Isherwood and Duckworth again gave Warringtoa the upper hand, but the Saints' for wards were mere than equal to the emergency and cleared their opponents out. tt Smack" broke away at centre and transferred to Moores, who gained ground ' before handinz to Isherwood, The latter raced feat tap speed bat was brought down just on the wrong side of the line. Quickly the game was transferred to the other end and Boscow called upon. Briers was prominene just before half-line when the score sea's" nil ' , each. Taylor renewed hostilities,and St. Heletis replied with a couple of passing merestnents which were badly manouyre I. Foulkes, eraynor, and lisrnes shaped bet- ter a moment later, the latter running strongly before being pushed in touch. Sc. Helens attacked with great cl,termination and should certainly have scored but all their advantages were lest by Foulkes who knocked on when he had a stood chime to drop a goal. J. Bete and Moeres changed the aspect of matters with a °leiter mevement towards the visitors' line. Moires kickse in- to the open and Duck worth tried a drop at goal which was nearly sueeeisful. Time was flying however and the home crowd was showing signs ot impatience at the fruitle sness of the struggle. The home backs played with commendable dash, though "Smack" was ill-sup- petted at times. On one 'cession he tricked his vis-a-vis and got clear away but could not pass Foulkes. There sires no-one to back him up and chance was thus lost. Cleat this time a misfortune befel St. Helens, Flynn having to leave the field through an injury. His loss robbed the visitors of the advantage they had had for. ward. Warrineton took advantage of this and made things lively in the Sr. Helens half. R Bate was almost in from his brother's pass. Then Moores made another good effnrt and finished up with a punt across ths goal. Tee ball was taken up smartly and beiag transferred to Dunkworth the latter ran in easily, amid rousing cheers. Holereft failed at goal. For the remaining five minutes the Saints had all their work cut out to keep the score from being increased, Traynor shining repeatedly on the defence. Warrington were left winners of a very even game by one try to nil. RUNCORN v. SALFORD. RUNCORN LOSE MUER A. HARD GAME.

Runcorn opened the season, at the Irwell-lane enclo- sers, last Saturdey, when they met Salford in the Lan eashire Senior Leaeue. The day was beautifully fine— in fact a little too fine for the kind of sort. Though the match is by no means the "big draw" of the season, a large number of spectators lined the enclosure, and patronised the stands, close upon 4000 being present when Runcorn took the field at 3 30. The visitore,were Rotnewhat late, but at abut 345 the following teams faced each other, under the control of Mr. J. Smith, Widnes,whe refereed : Rancor • : Beck, S. if ; three quarters, C. Butterworth, P. Woods, T. Wilkinson, and T. Warder; halves, J. Jolly-, and J. Nickson ; forwards, A. Taylor, El Parma-, S. Walker, F. Gavter, W. Lightfoot, W. Bit. ley, 0. Hugh's, and F. Jameson. Selford : Back, Smith: three-quarters, T. Williams, Phillips, Eloskies, Bradley, Tnornas ; halves, Ivor Grey, and Griffiths ; forwards, J Williams, Moss' Gledhill, Rhapps, Heath, Brown, VVoldheld, and Dickson. Rhapps, (Salford), started off with a rousing kick to- wards his opponents left, and the opening of hostilities was received with cheers on all sides. Wilkinson rushed up and secured. During the scrimmage one of the Sal- ford men go: off-side, which advantage was well accoun- ted for by the homestera. Who worked steadily and irresistibly into the affections of the Belford men. For some tirno the whole of the Runcorn fifteen got well down hate the visitor; half, but Salford got away with an effective motion on tee left. Houehten was there, however, and back went the ball. Then followed some remarkable work on the part of the Rencorn pack. Just as it might have been effective, however, Rhappe was pulled up for roughness. Jolley was now censpicnoue, and secured several fair catches. Woods was nest res- ponsible for a smart piece of work, as intercepting the visfeore pees to the scoring wing, he got away, in fine style. bet Smith, the Salford back, was smart enough to collar him on the line. From the scrimmage Hughes got over the line, but Smith agaio saved his charge by tackling finely before the touch-down. An anxious time was now experienced by the visitors, and had the home team but a little more speed on the field nothing would have prevented them from scoring heavile. As it was, Smith had repeatedly to send les) touch to SAVO his charge, and on one occssion Was so hard preseed as to be compelled to throw over the dead ball use hind. Ivor Grey got a foit opening' but had evidently reckoned without Doughten. Walker then got over with a dribble and touched down, hut the whistle had just gone for some slight infringement on the part of Salford. Brown and Slums then broke away,and play was transferred for a few minutes te Runcorn quarters. Having driven the h mestere back, they again got off with a swift move- ment,and had a fair chance of scoring, but C. Butter- worth, who though but a young player, saw his opportunity and tackled beautifully grass- ing. his Man in a capital warmer. Jolley tri`vi to drop a goal but just failed, T. Wilkinson then got an opening but also failed. For the next few minutes Salford had a show to themselves, coming away on the right with a splendid bit of passing. Equally as good, however, was that which followed en the part of the Runcorn pack, who were awarded a Penalty, which Jolley neatly placed between the sticks, a performance that was hailed with frantic cheers. With a few minutes left to the interval things became exciting, and Salford made the going heavy. Williams (Salford) recelved a pass when in a good position ; and would undoubtedly heve got over the line, had not Ammon fetched him up with about one of the finest pieces of work accomplished daring the afternoen. It was only just in time too. Half-time score : —Runcorn, 1 goal (penalty) 2 punts : Salfori nil. The second half was opened by Farmer, and Runcorn once more pressed. Scrimmage followed scrim- mage and the pace got hotter and hotter. Jolley was collared but tried to bieak; away with the result that

div.head: COMMENTS.
div.p: COMMENTS.

Though defeatel the home team have nothing to he ashamed of. They playa] pluckily, steadily, and spiritedly tlarouehout. Their tackling was good, their tactics were capital ; bat they certainly did leek speed and it is to that deLict, and that alone, that their defest I can be attributed. Of the two sets of forwards, though the Salford neck were the heaviest, Ruacorn pet in ' equally as much work aril their work was of a better quality. The helves were about equal. The becks,well everyone knows Houghton ; so it would be a pity to compare them. About Smith, however, I must state that he was one of two things, eith-r a rattlina good speedy back,or fess a lucky fellow. I have not yet rein him often enough to judge which but if he always plays like thatehen he is a really good man and an acquisition. But, to proee el, the game was r ally a match between the threeqearterseeastways it was the superiority of the visiting te's that won the game • and that was only in respect to speed. As for tact C 3, 'Rancorti were equally as good,if not a little superior. On the whole the Let team lost ; and when the fact that auch a lot of money has been exp,nded in getting the Salford team toeoith is taken into consideration, one is compelled to think— (on form of course)—that it is poor value. True it was a win,and counts two points, but it was a lucky affair at best, and the winners have nothing to boast about. WIDNES DEFEAT MORECAMBE. On Saturday Morecambe were pitted again 4 Widnee. The sprightly Widnesians landed at Morecambs with an unbeaten certificate, and without Brennan, their cap- tain,their vice-captain. and Flesleeb But with such a powerful " A " team to draw upon, the vacaneies were readily filled with reelly capable men. On the other hand Morecambe had by no means their full strength at command. Gardner, the three-quarter, is ea the sick list, so is the once famous •1 Bratty " Holmes ; whilst Herbert Wilson persists in saying that be has retired from active service. Thus tsvo practically untried youngsters—T. A. Lamb and T. isersgmire—had to be placed in the three-quarter line, and from the forwards a trio of hard workers were missing—Coreth- waits, R. Jackson, and Wand. There was a pretty riff wind blowing down the field, and for the s-cead weak in successio o Elkin saw his opponents turn their baeks to it. The game hod not been going long before the Widnesiane get down Co the home end, where Batey had an unsuceessf al shot at goal. Blacow took play to midfield, where it continued for a trine' until Batey and Alec Martin cembmed in making a glorious mull that nearly let the seasiders experience what it is like to get a try. A capital swineine movement by the Widnes backs should have ended in Peacock crossing the line,bet he threw the ball over hie head. Altham 'mese 1 gather- ing the ball on his own line, and a try would have been the result had not the light weight, Lamb, gathered the precious oval unto himself. A motnent or two la'er Drummond threw over to Rispan, who " diddled "Her- bert Hadwea by pretending to pass to Peacock, and himself scered a try, which Batey did not improve. The nterval came round with the visitors enjoying a three points lead. When the struegle was rene wee there was ne noticeable improvement in the style of play. The home side by a determined rush and some smart play on the part of iltow aid Jackson raised hopes in the bosoms of their supporters, but those sell same hopes were soon le' Wed. Hardly had the crowd reoevered its breath before le-aeeeck got hold aud strolled over the Rue to ths evident amazement of the home centre three- quarters, who obligingly stood stock still whilst the Widnes man did thstrick. Batey made no mistake this time, and with eight points to their credit the visitors won without having allowed the home team to score.

NEW TON-LEIVILLO V. FIUDSONS (LIVERPOOL

COMBINATION), This na%tei came off at Newton, and a 3 it was the home team's Brat match under the au9picei of thet Liv Er. pool Combination' along with the fact that their oppo nonts were the champions last season, and winners of the Liverpool Shield, a vast amount of interest was centered in the encounter. The weather was all that could be dethei and there was a very good attendance. Mr. Blair of the Referee's Association was in command, and needless to say he very soon was in evidence at checking any unfair work, and the game al a cease-

vence was of a very pleasant deuription. Mr. Seth Hutchins m one of the vice-Presidents of the Newton club started the game amid applause, and Morrisey get- ting the ball pass al on well to his wing, wile went along in fine style, -nd Rnuelbotham centreing. G. Houghton came into possession and banged the ball past Easdale in fine style. The referm greatly to the disappointment of the ape :caters gave off-side. There wag new some lively work, both goalkeepers' having to save. Bu'lar was loudly applauded for some very tricky play g tting round 80/113 of his • opponents in quite his old time style. The referee again ha I t give tie Newton skipper off-sido when he was bmorning dangerous. McFarlane, the right back for Hudson'a' played well. The game was very exciting up to half time, but nit a point could eitner side get, and a blank sleet was the result when refreMments were served. The second half was fiercely contested and same lively incidents occurred, especially in the Hudson goal mout a. Easdale was certainly a t-•‘ at and gave a grand exhinition of goal-keeping. G. Houghton was within an ace of scorine in the last milinte, but kicked the ball a bit too far, and Easdale just managed to give a corner. Cunningham sent in a lon, shot that hit the Newton bar—a near thing. The referee blew the whistle with the ball hovering anout Easiale, with no goals having been registered, but Hudsons' on the play tieing lucky to escape with a draw. Without d eibt Newton have done a good thing in getting in the G-mhinvion, and will tmlng some of the fineit amateur Clubs in Lancashire down to the Nursery. Their oppon- ents on Saturday were a vary good team, and whav; was more were sportsmen in every sense of the word, never demurring at the referee's decision, and admitting , on the day's play that they were the inferior te irn, but of course remarked that two points would be down to th ir credh in the retutn game. All played well, and thus it wuld le tidar to individualise, but with , such games football should prosper at Newton and a few "gates" like Saturday's will be the means of pla :ing the club on a good financial footing. Only in- different suppor; has been our share in the past, but a goo I programme should bs the means of attracting the natives who should see by now that the Club needs all the supnort it can es% Oa Saturday another combina- tion game is down ta be played at Newton, Brombore Pool being the visitors and a good game will no doubt result when the hornesters play under the impression , that they will "bag a hearse" of points. CLUB PICNIC.

On Saturday afternoon, the members of the bowling club held at Mr, W. J. Hewitt', of the Gladstone Arms Inn, Church-street, Warrington,had their annual picnic. The place selected this year was the Joiner's Armt Hotel Croft, where they arrived about three o'clock. A main of bowls was afterwards commenced by the members, numbering 22, the game being eleven up and the limit three. The results were :—First prize, copper kettle, Harry Hankey ; second, timepiece, Edward Hewitt ; third, knives and folks, George Thorniley ; and seven other prizes. The members and their friends after ;va,rds partook of a knife and fork tea. The remainer of the evening was spent in a very convivial momner,songs and imtrumental music being well rendered.

BAPTISMAL REGENERATION. Sir,—Now that' Sursurn Cords" hang 3 his head in the dejection of defeat, it may affintd him some relief to solve the problem that exercises his mind se to the types of Protestant! produced by the Bible. As a matter of fact, the Bible does not prcduce the Ritualist. He is the product of the Church of England Prayer Beek, which is admitted to I!, a compromise between Protestanism and ROlllaalt3M, and the Ritualist works for all Ills worth, theßomanist section. With him, the Bible has little, if indeed any weight. It cannot be said either that the Bible produces the Unitarian, as he Seta no more store upon the scriptures than upon any other " good " brok. The Bible produces only Evangelical Protestants, and these whether in the Church of England, or amringiit the Nonconformists, are to all intents and purposes of " one faith." "Sursum Cords," wi I see that Prayer Book churchmen like the renegade "Quondam Schismaticutt," have no faith in the Bible when they seek to supersede its direct tea doing. The scriptures tell us plainly that "all have sinned, and come short of the knowledge of God ;" but "Quondam Schisnnaticus ' knows better, for he says it is not so. There it just ore ques- tion I should like to ask "Quondam Scbisrnaticus and it is this : If there are people who need rice convorsion it must surely be those who are born and brought up in a religious atmosphere, such as a clergy msn's home,and yet how is it, and why is it, that these very ch lrlren mostly go wrong ? S irely " Quon- dam Schismaticus " only needs to go a step further, and that is to embrace Romanisrn. Personally, I should never say a ward about Remaoism if it Con- tended itself with pushing its principles by moral suasion. But when I find it endeavouring to force its beliefs upon people who are opposed to it, and s 'eking to obtain territorial sway to further it ends then, re- membering how it has blight,d every country upon which it has fastened its superstitous dogmas, I feel impelled to combat its error, and to do my utmost to maintain the religious freedom of my country.— Tours, &c.,

Church of Rome believes that. S. C. is puzzled by the differences of opinion and of interpretation in the ranks of the free churches. He is I under the delusion that unity of spirit, spells uni• formity of methol, and thht our L,rd prayed for nal- ' formity net unity. I would commend him to read 1 Cor. au i and especially verses 4-7, "Now there are I diversities of gifcs, but the Fame spirit. And Vivre aro differences of a ministrations, but the same Lord, and there are diversities of operations but it is the same God which worketh all in all." Although there are in the free churches differences of adminis'ra- tion and aiversities of operations, there is but one spirit. I hold that there is more reel, spiritual and genuine union between the free churches, than there pesidv.ily can be in the Romisb church ; for the union that exists there is the union of surrendered minds, suppressed thought, of force, and of fuperstitious threats, arid is es far removed from that for which our Lord prayed as anything possibly could he. It is simply a pretenc3 of Unity. That, any one can prove, by observing the move- ments and reading the history of the limnish Church. The Rev. H. P. Hughes, President of th 3 Wesleyan Con- ference, Bey" that when visiting the continent he saw villages, where there were three and even four Roman Catho'ic Churches, belonging to different parties in the Church, standing apart from each other, and icing as bitter against each other, as it was possible for any sectaries to be. Bishop Hall says in his book on " The Peace of Rome " that there are no less than 300 differ- ences of opinion maintained in the Church of Rome. To exaggerrate the divisions of Protestants, and to claim absolute freedom from disunion among Papists, is what S.C. delights to do. But I cannot think he is blind to the existence of sects and parties in his church nor yet to the awful dig ,nion history reveals in her ranks Has be ever heard of the Arian disputes,which disturb,d his church for over 50 years ? or of Pope Vigilius, who came into conflict with the fifth General Council, and was ea-._oatmunicated ? Does he know anything of Pope Honorius I. who was I condemned for heresy, on the question of Monotheliem ? I Was Vs( re absolute unity in 1870 when the Pope WAS de- clared ? Did not 100 French and German big. Mops retire from the vatic in, rather than tike part in the promulgation of the Dogma? Was there not a schism once in the West in 1378, when the French cardinals elected Clement VI. in opposition to Urban VI., and for 50 years Elva division lasted, the astonished WIT ICI seeing sometimes as many as three Popes claiming the office ? Has not the Papal chair been vacant four times s nce 1268—each time for over two years, because the church was so divided that they could not agree on a successor? In the face of these facts of history how can S. C. claim infallibility for either Pope, Church, or Priest. S.C. believes in the figment of Apostolic succession. There is nothing in the Bible to warrant such a belief and Church history is fatal to the dogma. IS it not a proverb that some of the Roman Pontiffs were men of seandalous life. Pope Alexandria Borgia was one,s man whose infamous progeny were the shame of Christen- dom. " Fronde" in his Council of Trent says "he died of accidentally drinking a cup of poison which lie had mixed for anether."Jesult uriti re hire La hbe and Cement describe SOMA of the Popes as " monsters, heretics.mur- derers, robbers, tyrants,adultererrhand apost itei." John XII. was deposed for the crimes of heresy, simony, and most atrocious licenteousness. Cardinal and general of his'order St. Bonaventure, whom Lb, P- ones loaded with honours,in his commentary on the Apocalypse,rompares Rome to the harlot there mentioned for he said "Church dignities were bought and sold. Here, did the princ=,s and rulers of the Church assemble, dishonouring God be their incontinence,adherents ot Eatan,and plunderers of the flock of Christ." S•ronger words could not be used by the most bigoted Protestant,and we are unblushine.lr asked to believe that the succession was handed down through such foul characters ! Let S.C. explain these things for they are fatal to his theories and delusions, about the unity, purity and infallibility of his Church. Yours etc.,

The Rev. Canon Penrhyn, rector of Win wick, occupied the pulpit of Wargrave Cottrell on Sunday evening, and in r,ho course of his discourse referred in sympathetic terms to the death of the Empresi of Austris, reznarking that every civilised notion was horrified at the cowardly murder. He pointed out the lessons which might be learned from the sail end of the Empress, and re- marked that such enormities were brought about tor the purpose of teaching us the existence of an all seeing anti all powerful God.

div.head: DISASTROUS FA RM . FIRE AT E A RLESTO WN.
div.p: DISASTROUS FA RM . FIRE AT E A RLESTO WN.

A lire of a most destructive character broke out in the farm yard of Old Hay Farm, Earlestown. occupied by Mr. John Bridge, early on Saturday morning, and so rapid was its progress that seven stackn of hay and corn were very sosn destroyed or rendere I unfit for use. The stacks were all this year's produce, and were clustered together in the yard behind the farm buildings, two being in a Dutch barn, and the others within a very f-w yards of each other. About half-past two on Saturdny morning a signalman in a box close by the farm hal his attention drawn to an unusually large quantity of smoke which appearel to be issuing from the farm buildings, and afterwards a flame of fire con- vinced him there WAS something seriously wrong. He at, once left his box, and aroused the inmates of the farm, when it Was found that the stacks in the Dutch barn were in flames A telephonic message Was at once sent to Warrington for e.asistanee, and the brigade which was eng3ged at a fire when the message arrived, at once set off to Earlestown with the steam fire engine" Major.' and they reached the scene of the fire about four o'clock. Information was also sent to the Viaduct Works, Earlestown, and the brigade there promptly turned out, but they did not reach the farm until 4 27. The Warrington brigade were then at work, end doing what they could to subdue the flames. The fire, however, had got a firm hold, and the roof of the Dutch barn quickly fell in,show-re of spa-ks being scattered in all directions, and very soon the remaining stacks were all ablaze, with -the excep- tion of a.large stack of corn, which fortunately escaped injury. Inspector Morgan with several constables arrived on the scene, and they rendered assintance. hut Hy) services of the Viaduct works brigade not being mytired the men returned home. Great fears-were entertained that the barn which was filled with corn, might become involved and in fact the door did become ignited, hut the Warring- ton man s.uceeeded in warding oEf danger in this direction. One of Mr. Bridge's sons had a mirecu- lous escape from dea'h, as in the nick of time be stepped out of the way as one of the burning stacks toppled over on to spot where he had an instant before been standing. There was fortunately a plentiful supply of wat.,r. the canal being only a few yards away, and al- though the firemen worked hard to subdue the filmes, they had to leave two of the stacks to the mercy of the fire and direct their attention to the othera in order to prevent the flames spreading to !h corn stack and farm buildings. The scene dur- ing the height of the crmflsgration was magnificent end the glare was vieibls for miles around The fire was got under some time during the morning ble it was not until seven o'clock at night that the Warrington men considered it safe to leave the Premises, and they returned home. The burniig hay had to be watched all night, and during Sun- day the dense clouds of smoke pervaded the neigh- bonrhool, the ha l and straw having to be carted away and spread on the fields to burn itself out. Lwkily rain fell on Sunday and this greatly assis- ted in the quenching of the burning waste, The origin of the fire is not known, but the produce was insured. The loss is estimated at about .EBOO.

MR. WILSON RI, ACKLIIDGB at PARR HALL on. THURSDA.Y.—Advt. LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHRPIIRRDS, (WARRINGTON DISTRICT.) The quarterly meeting of the" Late Spring Rose Lodge,' took place on Saturday evening at the Bar- ley Mow,Market-street. W. M. William Sollory pre- sided, being supported in the vice-chair by D. M. Edward S. GleaVe. The statement of accounts was read end passed after the auditors (Messrs. Hill and Tilling) had certified their correctness. The report was very satisfactory showing the lodge to he in a healthy condition both numerically and financially. After the ordinary business the Presi- dent called upon P.P.C.S. Thomas Duckworth to make a presentation to P. M. George A. Tilling of a framed emblem of merit for services rendered to the lodge. Bro Duckworth in making the presenta- tion said it off ,rded him very great pleasure in be- ing called upon to make the pres ritation. He was pleased to see young men like Bro Tilling taking an interest in the workings of the lodge and Pass- ing through the various offices of the lodge and performing them so well. Bro Tilling had been very regular, punctual, and impartial, while going through the chairs and he hoped other young mem- bers would try to follow his example. In asking Bro. Tilling to accept this small token of respect he hoped that he would take it home and hang it in the most consoicious place in his house and that when he looked upon it, it would remind him of the happy hours he had spent and the many friends that he had made while going through the various offices of the lodge. These remarks were warmly supported by P.P.C.E James Parr, P.M. John Jones, P.M.vVilliam Parr, and P.M. Whitlow, secretory. Bro Tilling in reply thanked them for the very handsome present and for the expressions of good feeling towards him. He could assure them •hat he should still go on in the future as in the past and that whatever he could do to farther the intereS'S of the Lodge, and the Order in general he would do,
